title: Full Inseparability And Genuine Multipartite Entanglement Coincide For Finite-Mode Gaussian States
authors: Yu Yang, Yuhang Wang, Chunxiao Du, Shikun Zhang, Zheng Qin, Rui Li, Wenxiu Li, Hao Zhang, Zhisong Xiao
abstract: ArXiv:2609.10984v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For general mixed states, entanglement across every bipartition need not imply genuine multipartite entanglement (GME), because a biseparable decomposition may switch the separable cut from term to term. We prove that this convex ambiguity disappears for Gaussian states of finitely many bosonic modes. More generally, for any finite family of partitions, a Gaussian density operator in the trace-norm-closed convex class generated by states separable across those partitions is already separable across one fixed partition in the family. Only the target is Gaussian; a valid decomposition may be continuous and may contain arbitrary non-Gaussian states. Thus full inseparability and GME coincide, Gaussian k-separability and k-producibility reduce to fixed-partition tests, and party-wise tensor powers cannot activate GME from a biseparable Gaussian state. The proof combines a spectral selector with a holomorphic rigidity argument that converts one product vector in the square-root range of a Gaussian state into a block-local covariance certificate. The result shows that partition mixing, a generic mixed-state mechanism, adds no new exact finite-mode Gaussian states.
tldr: The paper proves that for finite-mode Gaussian states, full inseparability (entanglement across every bipartition) coincides with genuine multipartite entanglement, removing the convex mixing ambiguity present for general mixed states.
motivation: For general mixed states, entanglement across all bipartitions does not imply genuine multipartite entanglement because biseparable decompositions may switch the separable cut from term to term. Whether this ambiguity persists for Gaussian states was an open question.
method: The proof combines a spectral selector with a holomorphic rigidity argument that converts one product vector in the square-root range of a Gaussian state into a block-local covariance certificate. Only the target state is required to be Gaussian; the decomposition may be continuous and contain arbitrary non-Gaussian states.
result: It is shown that any Gaussian density operator in the trace-norm-closed convex class generated by states separable across a finite family of partitions is already separable across one fixed partition in the family. Consequently, full inseparability and GME coincide, Gaussian k-separability and k-producibility reduce to fixed-partition tests, and party-wise tensor powers cannot activate GME from a biseparable Gaussian state.
conclusion: Partition mixing, a generic mixed-state mechanism, adds no new exact finite-mode Gaussian states. This simplifies the characterization of multipartite entanglement in continuous-variable Gaussian systems and tightens the connection between full inseparability and genuine multipartite entanglement.

The authors prove that for Gaussian states of finitely many bosonic modes, this convex ambiguity disappears. Specifically, they show that for any finite family of partitions, a Gaussian density operator that lies in the trace-norm-closed convex hull of states separable across those partitions must itself be separable across one fixed partition in the family. title: Full-Rank Noise Forbids Long-Range Entanglement Swapping
authors: Xuan Du Trinh, Nicholas Pardave, Angie Huang, Xiangyi Meng, Nengkun Yu
abstract: ArXiv:2609.11021v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum repeaters extend entanglement by swapping noisy elementary links. We prove that full-rank noise forbids this at long range: for any entangled full-rank two-qubit link, there is a finite depth beyond which no end-to-end entanglement can be established regardless of the measurement outcomes on intermediate qubits, even under any adaptive postselected strategy. This limit is set by one spectral parameter of the link, giving a no-go criterion for repeater routing. In contrast, we construct link state families of rank three and rank two that admit postselected measurement outcome branches of exponentially small probability but with strictly positive concurrence at every finite depth. Swapping experiments on a superconducting processor show that links of equal initial concurrence but different rank behave differently under postselected swapping. In the language of many-body physics, the chain is a matrix-product density operator, and full-rank bonds forbid long-range localizable entanglement, while rank-deficient bonds can sustain it.
tldr: Full-rank noise in elementary links sets a hard limit on long-range entanglement swapping, forbidding end-to-end entanglement beyond a finite depth even with adaptive postselection.
motivation: Quantum repeaters rely on entanglement swapping over noisy links, but it is unclear whether full-rank noise fundamentally prevents long-distance entanglement distribution.
method: The authors prove a no-go theorem using a spectral parameter of the link state, and construct rank-deficient link families that evade the limit; they also perform swapping experiments on a superconducting processor.
result: For any entangled full-rank two-qubit link there is a finite depth beyond which no end-to-end entanglement can be established, while rank-three and rank-two links can maintain positive concurrence at every finite depth under postselected branches.
conclusion: The work provides a no-go criterion for repeater routing and connects the phenomenon to localizable entanglement in matrix-product density operators, showing that full-rank bonds forbid long-range localizable entanglement.

title: Conditional-squeezing Gate In Superconducting Circuits
authors: Roman Schiaffino, Fernando C. Lombardo, Juan Pablo Paz
abstract: ArXiv:2609.10655v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present an implementation of a conditional-squeezing gate that squeezes a SQUID-terminated resonator mode along a direction determined by the state of a dispersively coupled qubit. This gate generalizes the controlled-squeezing gate [Phys. Rev. A , 042606 (2025)], and relies on a refocusing technique to suppress unwanted effects arising from slowly varying time-dependent terms in the Hamiltonian during the state-dependent parametric resonance required for the operation. As an application, we use the gate to encode an arbitrary qubit state into superpositions of single- and two-mode squeezed states of the resonator. These non-Gaussian states enable error-detectable encoding through parity measurements. We show that refocusing substantially improves the encoding fidelity, which is ultimately limited by Kerr nonlinearities and dissipation in realistic implementations. For experimentally optimistic values of the nonlinearities and decay rates, we obtain encoding fidelities above 0.99 for arbitrary input qubit states. Our results provide a route toward extending this scheme to the generation of higher-order superpositions of squeezed states (a class of rotation-symmetric bosonic codes) using a control qudit.
tldr: The paper proposes and analyzes a conditional-squeezing gate in superconducting circuits that uses a dispersively coupled qubit to squeeze a resonator mode, enabling encoding of qubit states into non-Gaussian squeezed-state superpositions for error-detectable bosonic codes.
motivation: Controlled generation of non-Gaussian states is essential for bosonic quantum error correction, but practical implementations suffer from unwanted Hamiltonian terms and decoherence.
method: They implement a state-dependent parametric resonance with a refocusing technique to suppress slow time-dependent terms, and use the gate to encode arbitrary qubit states into superpositions of single- and two-mode squeezed states, analyzing fidelity limits from Kerr nonlinearities and dissipation.
result: Refocusing substantially improves encoding fidelity, reaching above 0.99 for optimistic experimental parameters, with performance ultimately limited by Kerr nonlinearities and decay.
conclusion: The scheme provides a viable route toward higher-order squeezed-state superpositions and rotation-symmetric bosonic codes using a control qudit in superconducting circuits.

title: Bargmann Invariants Are Insufficient For Complete Local-Unitary Orbit Discrimination
abstract: ArXiv:2609.11090v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Bargmann invariants constructed from a bipartite density operator and its two lifted marginals are polynomial invariants of local-unitary conjugation. We determine the precise information encoded in these invariants. Whenever one subsystem is a qubit, the ordinary marginal-word family determines the full spectrum of the partial transpose and hence decides whether the state has the positive-partial-transpose property. In [MATH] and [MATH] systems, this yields complete separability criteria. For the two-qubit system, a finite subfamily additionally separates local-unitary orbits, and a finite extension generates the polynomial invariant ring. These three tasks already diverge for qubit-qutrit states: we exhibit full-rank, locally maximally mixed states that agree on all ordinary marginal-word invariants yet have different operator-Schmidt ranks, together with a quartic correlation invariant that separates them. When both local dimensions are at least three, the analogous collapse on the locally maximally mixed sector produces isospectral pairs consisting of one separable state and one entangled state with negative partial transpose. The ordinary Bargmann algebra therefore coincides with the full local unitary invariant ring if and only if both subsystems are qubits. The missing data are geometric: they encode the placement of global eigenspaces relative to the tensor-product decomposition.
tldr: The paper characterizes Bargmann invariants as local-unitary polynomial invariants and shows they fully determine PPT and separability only when one subsystem is a qubit, failing for higher-dimensional bipartite states.
motivation: Local unitary invariants are central to entanglement classification and detection, but it was unclear exactly how much information the Bargmann invariant family encodes about bipartite quantum states.
method: The authors construct Bargmann invariants from a bipartite density operator and its lifted marginals, then analyze marginal-word families, partial transpose spectra, invariant rings, and explicit counterexample states.
result: For qubit subsystems the ordinary marginal-word family determines the partial transpose spectrum and yields complete separability criteria; for qubit-qutrit and larger local dimensions, states agreeing on all ordinary Bargmann invariants can have different operator-Schmidt ranks or different separability properties.
conclusion: The ordinary Bargmann algebra coincides with the full local unitary invariant ring if and only if both subsystems are qubits, with the missing information being geometric data about global eigenspace placement relative to the tensor-product decomposition.

title: Demonstration Of A Logical Bell-state Measurement Beyond The Linear-optical Limit
authors: Shreya Kumar, Simon D. Rei{\ss}, Peter van Loock, Stefanie Barz
abstract: ArXiv:2609.10698v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fault tolerance is essential for scalable quantum technologies and is enabled by quantum error-correction codes. Bell-state measurements (BSMs) are a fundamental building block for modern quantum technologies such as measurement-based quantum computation and fusion-based quantum computation, as well as quantum networks. Therefore, performing BSMs on error-corrected qubits is a necessary step for achieving fault tolerance in these applications. In this work, we realise a logical BSM using linear optics, based on a two-qubit repetition code, an instance of a quantum parity code that allows detection of bit-flip errors, and experimentally achieve a mean success probability of (70.8 +/- 0.4)%. While standard linear-optical BSMs are fundamentally limited to a maximum success probability of 50%, this increased success probability enables higher secure key rates in quantum communication and facilitates the generation of large graph states for quantum computation. Since fault-tolerant schemes require error-correction codes regardless, this improvement comes at no additional resource overhead. Our results demonstrate that error-correction codes can be used to surpass the linear-optics limit of BSMs, which is an important step towards practical, fault-tolerant, and scalable photonic quantum technologies.
tldr: The paper experimentally demonstrates a logical Bell-state measurement using a two-qubit repetition code in linear optics, achieving a mean success probability of 70.8%, which surpasses the fundamental 50% linear-optical limit.
motivation: Fault-tolerant quantum technologies require Bell-state measurements on error-corrected qubits, but standard linear-optical BSMs are limited to 50% success probability, hindering scalable photonic quantum computation and communication.
method: The authors implement a logical BSM based on a two-qubit repetition (quantum parity) code that detects bit-flip errors, using linear optics and measuring the mean success probability.
result: They achieve a mean success probability of (70.8 +/- 0.4)%, exceeding the 50% linear-optical limit without additional resource overhead since error correction is already needed for fault tolerance.
conclusion: This shows that error-correction codes can enhance BSM success probabilities, enabling higher secure key rates and larger graph states, and represents an important step toward practical fault-tolerant photonic quantum technologies.

title: Walking Floquet Code Circuits For Zero-overhead Leakage Reduction
authors: Hanna Westerheim, Kaavya Sahay, Shruti Puri
abstract: ArXiv:2609.10666v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Leakage, occurring when a qubit undetectably exits the computational subspace, poses a significant challenge for quantum error correction by inducing correlated errors in space and time. These correlations reduce both the code threshold and the effective code distance. To address this challenge, we introduce two zero-overhead walking circuits for the honeycomb Floquet code (hFC), termed the swirling and sliding circuits, which periodically remove leakage while dynamically protecting logical qubits via a schedule of anticommuting two-body measurements. Unlike previous dynamic circuits for the hFC, ours preserves the distance to Pauli errors. We further study their performance under leakage and find that, for two leakage noise models, they may correct as many leakage errors as Pauli errors, improving on the more widely known walking surface code. Through numerical simulation, we observe that finite-error-rate performance under leakage is strongly influenced by entropic effects, producing a pronounced waterfall regime in which the logical error rate decreases much more rapidly with physical error rate than the expected distance-limited scaling. In this regime, even when asymptotic predictions suggest otherwise, the hFC can outperform the same-distance walking surface code in error rates and sub-threshold logical error scaling.
tldr: The paper introduces zero-overhead walking circuits for the honeycomb Floquet code that periodically remove leakage while preserving distance to Pauli errors and improving logical error rates under leakage.
motivation: Leakage is a major obstacle for quantum error correction because it creates correlated errors in space and time, reducing thresholds and effective distance. Existing dynamic circuits for the honeycomb Floquet code did not preserve distance to Pauli errors.
method: The authors design two walking Floquet code circuits, termed swirling and sliding, based on schedules of anticommuting two-body measurements. They numerically simulate performance under two leakage noise models and compare with the walking surface code.
result: For the considered leakage models, the walking Floquet code circuits can correct as many leakage errors as Pauli errors, improving on the walking surface code. Numerical simulations reveal a pronounced waterfall regime where logical error rates drop faster than distance-limited scaling, allowing the hFC to outperform same-distance surface codes sub-threshold.
conclusion: Zero-overhead walking circuits provide a promising route to leakage-resilient Floquet code architectures, and entropic effects can lead to better-than-expected finite-error-rate performance.

title: Floquet Majorana Xyz Codes With Tunable Logical Dynamics
abstract: ArXiv:2609.10683v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We construct Floquet codes from the Majorana XYZ subsystem code with local realizations both in qubits and directly in microscopic Majorana modes with lattice size [MATH]. For a three-step cycle, odd [MATH] supports one static logical qubit, whereas even [MATH] supports two. For even [MATH] with [MATH], both logical qubits admit time-independent Pauli representatives. For [MATH], by contrast, one Pauli of the second logical qubit remains fixed throughout the cycle, while every representative of its conjugate must evolve through the measurement cycle. This distinction follows from a parity-dependent algebraic obstruction and disappears when the cycle is reduced to two steps, which restores a fully static logical pair. Thus, the same encoded logical degree of freedom can be switched between static and partially dynamical forms by the measurement schedule. With one open direction, suitable protocols can be implemented using only local Majorana parity measurements. To our knowledge, this is the first Floquet-code family with both a local qubit representation and a direct microscopic Majorana realization.

method: The authors build three-step measurement cycles from the Majorana XYZ subsystem code, analyze logical Pauli representatives, and identify a parity-dependent algebraic obstruction that governs static versus dynamical logical qubits.
result: Odd lattice size supports one static logical qubit, even lattice size supports two; for certain even sizes one logical qubit becomes partially dynamical, while reducing the cycle to two steps restores a fully static logical pair.
conclusion: This is claimed to be the first Floquet-code family with both a local qubit representation and a direct microscopic Majorana realization, enabling switchable static/dynamical logical degrees of freedom via local Majorana parity measurements.

title: Distributed Variational Quantum Computing With Deterministic Entanglement Tuning
authors: Ilhwan Kim, Yong-Su Kim, Kwang Jo Lee, Hyukjoon Kwon, Yosep Kim, Hyang-Tag Lim
abstract: ArXiv:2609.10932v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Distributed quantum computing offers a scalable route to quantum information processing by entangling spatially separated processors. Although gate teleportation enables universal computation across distributed nodes, it requires repeated consumption of high-fidelity Bell pairs, ancillary qubits, and real-time feedforward, which imposes significant overhead and reduces fidelity. However, many variational quantum algorithms do not demand full universality; rather, they rely on sufficient expressibility to explore solution spaces effectively. Building on this, we propose a distributed variational quantum computing protocol based on deterministic entanglement tuning. In contrast to probabilistic filtering, our approach deterministically modulates pre-shared entanglement using only local operations and classical communication. We validate the protocol through a proof-of-principle experiment by estimating ground-state energies of the He-H[MATH] molecule and the Schwinger model, showing that diverse entanglement levels can be engineered to match problem-specific requirements. Our results suggest a practical alternative for near-term distributed quantum applications.
tldr: A distributed variational quantum computing protocol uses deterministic entanglement tuning via LOCC, validated by estimating ground-state energies of a molecule and a lattice model.
motivation: Distributed quantum computing via gate teleportation demands repeated high-fidelity Bell pairs, ancillary qubits, and real-time feedforward, which imposes overhead; variational algorithms need only sufficient expressibility, not full universality.
method: Pre-shared entanglement is deterministically modulated using only local operations and classical communication, avoiding probabilistic filtering, and the protocol is tested in a proof-of-principle experiment estimating ground-state energies.
result: Diverse entanglement levels can be engineered to match problem-specific requirements, demonstrating that deterministic entanglement tuning supports near-term distributed variational quantum applications.
conclusion: The approach offers a practical alternative to gate-teleportation-based distributed quantum computing by tuning entanglement deterministically, with potential for near-term implementations.

title: Engineered Two-photon Dissipative Confinement Of A Kerr-cat Qubit Using Sisis Quantum Circuit Refrigerator
authors: Shumpei Masuda, Tsuyoshi Yamamoto, Shuji Nakamura, Daichi Sugiyama, Akiyoshi Tomonaga
abstract: ArXiv:2609.11034v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Kerr-cat qubits realized in periodically driven superconducting nonlinear resonators are a promising platform for quantum information processing with biased noise. Pure dephasing in such systems induces leakage out of the qubit subspace, motivating the use of quantum circuit refrigeration (QCR) to remove excess excitations. While conventional superconductor--insulator--normal-metal--insulator--superconductor (SINIS)-based QCRs can suppress leakage via single-photon absorption, they also enhance QCR-induced phase-flip errors. Here we investigate a QCR based on a superconductor--insulator--superconductor--insulator--superconductor (SISIS) junction coupled to a Kerr parametric oscillator (KPO). We show that a SISIS-based QCR can operate in a regime where single-photon processes are suppressed while two-photon absorption dominates. As a result, the proposed SISIS-based QCR achieves strong suppression of dephasing-induced leakage while substantially reducing the increase in phase-flip errors associated with QCR operation. These results demonstrate that the proposed SISIS-based QCR provides an effective approach for mitigating leakage while limiting QCR-induced phase-flip errors in Kerr-cat qubits.
tldr: A SISIS-based quantum circuit refrigerator using two-photon absorption suppresses dephasing-induced leakage in Kerr-cat qubits while reducing QCR-induced phase-flip errors.
motivation: Kerr-cat qubits suffer leakage from pure dephasing, and conventional SINIS-based QCRs mitigate leakage but worsen phase-flip errors, motivating a two-photon-dominant refrigeration scheme.
method: The authors theoretically analyze a superconductor-insulator-superconductor-insulator-superconductor (SISIS) junction coupled to a Kerr parametric oscillator, engineering a regime where single-photon processes are suppressed and two-photon absorption dominates.
result: The proposed SISIS-based QCR strongly suppresses dephasing-induced leakage while substantially reducing the increase in phase-flip errors compared to single-photon QCR operation.
conclusion: SISIS-based quantum circuit refrigeration provides an effective approach for mitigating leakage in Kerr-cat qubits while limiting QCR-induced phase-flip errors, benefiting biased-noise quantum information processing.

title: Finite-blockade Dynamics Of A Three-qubit Ccz Gate In Neutral-atom Arrays
abstract: ArXiv:2609.11159v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a theoretical study of finite-blockade dynamics in a symmetric three-neutral-atom system, providing a framework for understanding high-fidelity multiqubit quantum operations. The transition from the finite- to the strong-blockade regime is systematically investigated to examine the effects of finite Rydberg blockade. Using a single Gaussian laser pulse, we analyze the complete gate dynamics while explicitly accounting for population leakage into non-computational Rydberg states. By exploiting the permutation symmetry of the system, we construct a symmetry-adapted Hamiltonian that reduces the computational complexity while preserving the exact dynamics. This enables a systematic investigation of the interplay among the Rabi frequency, laser detuning, and Rydberg blockade strength, leading to the identification of optimal operating regimes with high fidelity, fast gate operation, and suppressed leakage. We further quantify the dominant error mechanisms, including phase errors, population leakage, and finite Rydberg-state lifetimes, and evaluate their impact on the gate fidelity. Our results demonstrate experimentally accessible high-fidelity gate operation and provide practical guidelines for multi-qubit quantum computing.

title: Quantum Random Access Memory Implementation Using Photon-Photon Interaction In Rydberg Atomic Ensemble
abstract: ArXiv:2609.11333v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum random access memory (qRAM) is crucial for overcoming data-loading bottlenecks in quantum machine learning; however, current physical implementations face severe scalability constraints. Traditional fanout designs demand exponential decoherence-prone gates, while bucket-brigade schemes require highly error-prone active switches. Motivated by these limitations, we propose a scalable qRAM architecture that fundamentally replaces active nodes with phase-encoded quantum walkers. Our methodology maps a discrete-time quantum walk onto a cavity quantum electrodynamics framework utilizing an electromagnetically induced transparency (EIT)-based Rydberg atomic ensemble. Inside hollow-core waveguides, strong Rydberg dipole-dipole interactions and a solenoidal magnetic field create a robust routing operator. This operator imparts precise, polarization-dependent phase shifts, steering circularly polarized probe pulses to target memory cells. Our results demonstrate that operating within a strong control field regime suppresses emergent spatial attenuation, ensuring cumulative transmission probabilities for highly scaled memory addresses. Ultimately, this parallelized architecture successfully optimizes spatial resources to static gates and temporal complexity to an optimal logarithmic scale of [MATH] by requiring [MATH] physical walkers, establishing a practical, fault-tolerant hardware pathway for advanced quantum computation implementations.

motivation: Current qRAM implementations face scalability constraints because fanout designs require exponentially many decoherence-prone gates and bucket-brigade schemes rely on error-prone active switches.
method: Maps a discrete-time quantum walk onto a cavity QED framework with an EIT-based Rydberg atomic ensemble, using strong Rydberg dipole-dipole interactions and a solenoidal magnetic field to create polarization-dependent phase shifts for routing probe pulses.

title: Information-Theoretic Characterization Of Macroscopic Chaos Emerging From The Chemical Master Equation
abstract: ArXiv:2609.11340v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Open chemical reaction networks exhibit stochastic concentration dynamics at finite system sizes, whereas their macroscopic limit is governed by deterministic rate equations that can display chaos. In this Letter, we show theoretically that a rate of information loss constructed from two-time mutual information recovers the Kolmogorov-Sinai entropy in the deterministic limit. We verify this result through numerical simulations of a Markov jump process for a three-species system involving seven reactions.
tldr: The paper shows that an information loss rate built from two-time mutual information recovers the Kolmogorov-Sinai entropy in the deterministic limit of stochastic chemical reaction networks.
motivation: Open chemical reaction networks exhibit stochastic concentration dynamics at finite system sizes, while their macroscopic limit can display deterministic chaos; connecting information-theoretic measures to classical chaos is thus of interest.
method: The authors construct a rate of information loss from two-time mutual information in the chemical master equation and compare it to the Kolmogorov-Sinai entropy, verifying the result via numerical simulations of a Markov jump process for a three-species system with seven reactions.
result: The information loss rate matches the Kolmogorov-Sinai entropy in the deterministic macroscopic limit, providing an information-theoretic characterization of macroscopic chaos.
conclusion: This work links stochastic master-equation descriptions of chemical kinetics to deterministic chaotic dynamics through an information-theoretic quantity.

The central theoretical result is that a rate of information loss, constructed from the two-time mutual information between the system's state at two different times, converges to the Kolmogorov-Sinai (KS) entropy in the deterministic limit. This establishes a direct link between a stochastic information-theoretic quantity and a fundamental measure of chaos. The authors verify this result numerically using a three-species chemical system involving seven reactions, simulating the Markov jump process and comparing the information loss rate to the KS entropy of the corresponding deterministic system. The work bridges stochastic thermodynamics, information theory, and nonlinear dynamics, suggesting that information loss can serve as a robust indicator of chaos in chemical networks.

title: On-chip Squeezed Light In The Audio Frequency Band
authors: Xuezhi Zhu, Yunyun Cao, Rui Liu, Yaya He, Fan Zhang, Yaqing Zhang, Shiwei Du, Meihong Wang, Xiaoshun Jiang, Xiaolong Su
abstract: ArXiv:2609.11004v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Squeezed light in the audio-frequency band is a key resource for quantum metrology and quantum sensing. However, realizing stable audio-frequency squeezed light on integrated photonic platforms remains challenging due to technical noise and the difficulty of scalable phase referencing. Here, we demonstrate on-chip generation of audio-band two-mode squeezed states down to 60 Hz in a silica microcavity. To enable phase-stable operation without directly locking fragile quantum modes, we develop a coherent-comb control method in which a weak electro-optic reference comb co-propagates with the vacuum at the quantum frequency modes in an orthogonal polarization. This scheme provides quadrature measurement and long-timescale phase stability, thereby enabling covariance-matrix reconstruction. We verify the entanglement with the positive partial transposition criterion, which confirms inseparability via a minimum symplectic eigenvalue of 0.395 ([MATH]). Our results establish an experimentally accessible route toward on-chip phase-stable audio-band squeezing and support the scalable framework for continuous-variable quantum information processing with integrated photonics.
tldr: On-chip generation of audio-band two-mode squeezed states down to 60 Hz in a silica microcavity using coherent-comb phase control.
motivation: Audio-frequency squeezed light is a key resource for quantum metrology and sensing, but stable on-chip generation remains challenging due to technical noise and scalable phase referencing.
method: A weak electro-optic reference comb co-propagates with vacuum at the quantum frequency modes in an orthogonal polarization, enabling quadrature measurement, long-timescale phase stability, and covariance-matrix reconstruction; entanglement is verified via the positive partial transposition criterion.
result: The minimum symplectic eigenvalue of 0.395 confirms inseparability, and the scheme achieves stable audio-band squeezing down to 60 Hz on an integrated photonic platform.
conclusion: The results establish an experimentally accessible route toward on-chip phase-stable audio-band squeezing and support scalable continuous-variable quantum information processing with integrated photonics.

title: Quantum-RAM Implementation Using Multiple Interacting Rydberg-Blockaded Eit Systems
abstract: ArXiv:2609.11344v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose a novel theoretical architecture for implementing a quantum random access memory (qRAM) based on quantum random walks in a Rydberg blockaded atomic ensemble utilizing multilevel Electromagnetically Induced Transparency (EIT). Unlike previous approaches that rely on geometric phase gates in solid-state or trapped ion systems, our scheme harnesses the strong, coherent dipole dipole interactions between Rydberg atoms to achieve high-fidelity phase control of photonic qubits without the need for cryogenic temperatures. By generating conditional phase shifts through cross-phase modulation in multiple lambda-type EIT systems, we realize the controlled unitary operations requisite for an efficient qRAM. In the proposed architecture, Zeeman splitting is used to engineer a set of parallel lambda systems in a cavity, where pairs of magnetic sublevels of the ground state are coupled to highly excited Rydberg states via circularly polarized laser pulses. These Rydberg excited EIT systems serve as the elementary phase gates that form the nodes of a binary tree enabling quantum random walking. Address and data qubits are encoded into distinct probe fields and coherently mapped into the metastable atomic states, where their interactions within the EIT medium generate conditional phases required for state-selective routing. The system uses [MATH] layers of cold alkali atoms to form an [MATH]-level binary tree of Rydberg nodes connected to [MATH] cavity-trapped memory atoms, operated by [MATH] laser pulses acting as quantum walkers and address units. Our scheme offers a scalable, reducing operational complexity to [MATH] and highly coherent pathway toward photonic qRAM, exploiting collective Rydberg interactions to realize programmable, parallel entangling operations in an atomic ensemble.
tldr: The paper proposes a theoretical architecture for photonic quantum random access memory (qRAM) using Rydberg-blockaded multilevel EIT systems in a cold atomic ensemble.
motivation: Efficient qRAM is a key component for scalable quantum computing, but existing approaches rely on solid-state or trapped-ion geometric phase gates that often require cryogenic temperatures and complex control.
method: The scheme uses Zeeman splitting to create parallel lambda-type EIT systems in a cavity, where Rydberg-mediated dipole-dipole interactions generate conditional phase shifts for controlled unitary operations, forming a binary tree of phase gates for quantum random walks.
result: The architecture coherently maps address and data qubits into metastable atomic states and achieves state-selective routing through cross-phase modulation, reducing operational complexity to a polynomial scaling while maintaining high fidelity without cryogenics.
conclusion: The proposal offers a scalable, highly coherent pathway toward programmable photonic qRAM by exploiting collective Rydberg interactions in atomic ensembles, though it remains a theoretical design awaiting experimental validation.

title: Threshold Behavior Of Zx And Zy Surface Codes Under Circuit-Level Biased And Crosstalk Noise
abstract: ArXiv:2609.10876v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Studying the threshold behavior of surface codes under biased noise models is an active area of research. Previous work Tuckett et al. (2018), using an optimal tensor-network decoder, demonstrated that replacing [MATH]-type stabilizers with [MATH]-type stabilizers significantly improves the surface code threshold under code-capacity level dephasing noise. In this work, we construct and study a [MATH] surface code by replacing the [MATH]-type stabilizers with [MATH]-type stabilizers. We compare it with the standard [MATH] surface code under circuit-level Pauli-[MATH] biased noise, with and without an additional gate-based [MATH] crosstalk noise. We find that for the [MATH] surface code, the [MATH]-memory threshold increases monotonically with bias while the [MATH]-memory threshold decreases and saturates. For the [MATH] surface code, the [MATH]-memory threshold is nearly constant across all bias values. The [MATH]-memory thresholds of the [MATH] and [MATH] codes are consistent within the uncertainty. Adding [MATH] crosstalk reduces the [MATH]-memory threshold beyond the fitting uncertainty while leaving the [MATH] memory threshold largely unaffected. The choice of CNOT ordering redistributes threshold performance between the two logical memories. Our work extends prior observations from code-capacity level noise to circuit-level noise. It also indicates the need for decoders capable of jointly reasoning over correlated syndrome information so that tailored stabilizer structures could be fully utilized for quantum error correction.
tldr: The paper constructs a ZX surface code by replacing X-type stabilizers with Z-type ones and compares its circuit-level threshold behavior against the standard ZY surface code under biased Pauli-Z noise and gate-based ZZ crosstalk.
motivation: Prior work (Tuckett et al. 2018) showed that tailoring stabilizer structure to biased noise improves thresholds at the code-capacity level, but it was unclear whether these gains survive realistic circuit-level noise, especially with correlated crosstalk errors.
method: Using circuit-level noise models with tunable Pauli-Z bias and an added gate-based ZZ crosstalk channel, the authors simulate Z-memory and X-memory thresholds of ZX and ZY surface codes and compare them under different CNOT orderings.
result: For the ZY code the Z-memory threshold grows monotonically with bias while the X-memory threshold decreases and saturates; the ZX code shows a nearly constant X-memory threshold, with cross-consistent Z-memory thresholds between the two codes. Crosstalk notably degrades the Z-memory threshold of the ZY code but leaves the ZX memory largely unaffected, and CNOT ordering redistributes performance between logical memories.
conclusion: The code-capacity advantages of bias-tailored stabilizer structures only partially persist at circuit level, highlighting the need for decoders that jointly exploit correlated syndrome information to fully leverage tailored codes.

title: Probing The Error-Mitigation Threshold With Matrix Product States
authors: Jia-Yao Zhao, Zhi-Yuan Wei, Michael J. Gullans
abstract: ArXiv:2609.10929v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum error mitigation relies on accurate noise characterization, but mismatches between the actual and characterized noise can be amplified and drive a sharp threshold between successful and failed mitigation. In random circuits, this threshold maps onto a random-field Ising transition, but previous exact numerics were limited to small one-dimensional and all-to-all systems, leaving explicit two-dimensional architectures unresolved. We develop a fixed-bond-dimension matrix-product-state method for the replicated transfer dynamics that extends threshold calculations beyond exact propagation while retaining the finite-size signatures of the transition. At system sizes beyond previous exact studies, we recover the predicted absence of a threshold for quenched disorder in 1D, obtain a sharper annealed all-to-all critical point, and resolve architecture-dependent finite-depth thresholds in 2D square and heavy-hex circuits. These results establish replicated tensor-network dynamics as a practical tool for probing error-mitigation thresholds in large and higher-dimensional noisy circuits.
tldr: The paper develops a fixed-bond-dimension matrix product state method to compute error-mitigation thresholds in large and two-dimensional noisy random circuits, where the threshold maps onto a random-field Ising transition.
motivation: Quantum error mitigation can fail sharply when characterized noise mismatches actual noise, but previous exact numerics were limited to small one-dimensional and all-to-all systems, leaving two-dimensional architectures unresolved.
method: The authors simulate replicated transfer dynamics using a fixed-bond-dimension matrix product state approach, extending threshold calculations beyond exact propagation while retaining finite-size signatures of the transition.
result: At sizes beyond previous exact studies, they recover the predicted absence of a threshold for quenched disorder in 1D, obtain a sharper annealed all-to-all critical point, and resolve architecture-dependent finite-depth thresholds in 2D square and heavy-hex circuits.
conclusion: Replicated tensor-network dynamics is established as a practical tool for probing error-mitigation thresholds in large and higher-dimensional noisy circuits.

title: Low-cost Algorithm-to-execution Framework For Surface-code Quantum Computing
authors: Yunxin Tang, Zixuan Huo, Junxiang Huang, Zhou You, Zhirao Wang, Zhenai Ding, Yumeng Zeng, Yangyu Lu, Yiming Huang, Zongkang Zhang, Haipeng Xie, Ying Li, Jinzhao Sun, Xiao Yuan, Yuan Yao
abstract: ArXiv:2609.10965v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The execution of useful quantum algorithms on fault-tolerant processors requires more than a mapping from logical gates to encoded operations: the spatial organization, non-Clifford resource supply, and execution schedule must also be determined while keeping physical overhead within practical limits. Although the theoretical hierarchy from logical circuits to fault-tolerant operations is well established, these implementation choices are often specified and optimized separately. Here we develop a low-cost algorithm-to-execution framework for surface-code quantum computing. From hierarchical algorithm descriptions, it constructs dependency-preserving logical schedules and an executable workload capturing logical interactions, operation parallelism, and time-resolved non-Clifford demand, thereby linking logical computation to surface-code organization, resource-state preparation, and fault-tolerant execution in a traceable workflow. We apply the framework to twenty benchmark circuits across seven algorithm families and a hierarchically composed application-scale elliptic-curve discrete-logarithm workload. Physical costs vary substantially even for circuits with similar logical resource counts. Under our direct-rotation calibration, non-Clifford implementation selection reduces space-time volume by up to 241.5 times versus an all-synthesis baseline for the QAOA amplitude-amplification workload. Circuit-specific surface-code layouts reduce routed-latency estimates for all twenty benchmarks; thirteen also reduce space-time volume because communication savings outweigh added spatial overhead. These results show that low-cost fault-tolerant execution depends on computation scheduling and organization, not aggregate logical resource counts alone.
tldr: The paper presents a low-cost algorithm-to-execution framework for surface-code quantum computing that generates dependency-preserving schedules and optimizes non-Clifford resource supply and surface-code layouts to reduce physical overhead and space-time volume.
motivation: Executing useful quantum algorithms on fault-tolerant surface-code processors requires jointly determining logical scheduling, non-Clifford resource preparation, and surface-code organization, but these choices are often specified and optimized separately.
method: The framework builds hierarchical logical schedules and an executable workload from algorithm descriptions, capturing logical interactions, parallelism, and time-resolved non-Clifford demand, and links them to surface-code organization and resource-state preparation; it is evaluated on twenty benchmark circuits and a hierarchically composed elliptic-curve discrete-logarithm workload.
result: Physical costs vary substantially even for circuits with similar logical resource counts; under direct-rotation calibration, non-Clifford implementation selection reduces space-time volume by up to 241.5 times versus an all-synthesis baseline for QAOA amplitude amplification, and circuit-specific layouts reduce routed-latency estimates for all twenty benchmarks, with thirteen also reducing space-time volume.
conclusion: Low-cost fault-tolerant execution depends critically on computation scheduling and spatial organization rather than aggregate logical resource counts alone, motivating integrated algorithm-to-execution co-design for surface-code quantum computing.

title: Quantitative Fabrication-Error Reduction In Optomechanical Crystal Using Proximity Error Correction
authors: Pratip Ghosh, Anohita Mallick, Akshay K. Naik
abstract: ArXiv:2609.10741v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We demonstrate the use of proximity effect correction (PEC) in electron beam lithography (EBL) to improve the fabrication fidelity of dense photonic crystal structures. Monte Carlo simulations were employed to model electron scattering and determine the proximity function of the resist-substrate system. Based on this, a computational dose-modification scheme was implemented to compensate for nonuniform energy deposition during exposure. In addition, SEM-based image analysis was performed to quantitatively assess structural differences among uniformly exposed, manually dose-modified, and PEC-fabricated devices by comparing extracted geometries with the reference GDS design. The analysis revealed reduced dimensional deviation, improved spatial uniformity, and lower edge roughness in the PEC-corrected structures. These improvements resulted in a significantly enhanced optical quality factor in the fabricated photonic crystal cavities.
tldr: Proximity effect correction in electron beam lithography improves fabrication fidelity and optical quality factor of optomechanical photonic crystal cavities.
motivation: Fabrication imperfections degrade photonic crystal structures, limiting optical quality factors that are crucial for optomechanical and quantum photonic applications.
method: Monte Carlo simulation of electron scattering determined the proximity function, then a computational dose-modification scheme corrected nonuniform energy deposition; SEM image analysis compared geometries to the reference GDS design.
result: PEC-corrected devices showed reduced dimensional deviation, improved spatial uniformity, lower edge roughness, and significantly enhanced optical quality factor.
conclusion: Proximity error correction is an effective approach to mitigate fabrication errors in dense photonic crystals, potentially enabling higher-performance optomechanical devices.

title: Programmable Cmos Dac Operating In Cryogenic Environments For Controlling Superconducting Qubits
authors: A. Pelteku, D. Reitz, M. Covington, A. Frederick, H. Adebayo, K. D. Hillaire, N. Mitran, Z. Steffen, R. Schwartz, Z. Stegen, J. X. Przybysz, J. Yager, C. Walter, T. Graves, D. Meyer, J. Clark, G. R. Boyd, A. Pesetski
abstract: ArXiv:2609.10834v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper presents the design and test results of a CMOS current-based Digital to Analog Converter (DAC) that operates at cryogenic temperatures and that can be used to precisely control the amount of flux coupled to qubits or that can be used in the readout of superconducting circuits. The current pulse output can be controlled in terms of its amplitude, rise and fall slopes, via digital controls, and pulse width, via external triggers, while driving a superconducting circuit. The design has been implemented in a planar 90 nm CMOS process and test results closely match circuit predictions. The solution's wide degree of digital tunability affords potential application of the same device to many types of quantum circuits, beyond those discussed here. Due to the wide-ranging flexibility of digital CMOS control, we envision that this DAC design will enable the next generation of high-fidelity cryo-CMOS control architectures for superconducting qubits.
tldr: A cryogenic CMOS current-based DAC is designed and tested for precisely controlling flux and readout of superconducting qubits.
motivation: Superconducting qubit control requires low-noise, cryogenic-compatible electronics that can scale to many qubits without excessive room-temperature wiring.
method: The authors implemented a programmable current-steering DAC in a 90 nm CMOS process, with digital control of pulse amplitude, rise/fall slopes, and pulse width via external triggers, and characterized it at cryogenic temperatures while driving superconducting circuits.
result: Test results closely match circuit predictions, demonstrating wide digital tunability and suitability for flux biasing and readout of superconducting circuits.
conclusion: The DAC may enable next-generation cryo-CMOS control architectures for high-fidelity superconducting qubit systems and other quantum circuits.

title: Optimal T-Count For Block Encodings Of Fermionic And Spin Hamiltonians
authors: Jiaxin Ma, Kevin J. Joven, Yuan Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2609.11153v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We determine the non-Clifford [MATH]-gate cost of constructing block encodings of structured fermionic and spin Hamiltonians in a unitary Clifford[MATH] model, when arbitrarily many clean ancillas and unrestricted block-encoding subnormalization are allowed, but without mid-circuit measurements or classical feed-forward. Our main technical tool is an ancilla-compression theorem: any block encoding of an [MATH]-qubit operator with [MATH] clean ancillas and at most [MATH] [MATH] gates can be compressed to use at most [MATH] ancillas, without increasing the absolute error or [MATH]-count. For general second-quantized Hamiltonians with bounded one- and two-body coefficients, at operator-norm block-encoding error [MATH], a volume-covering argument combined with circuit counting gives the worst-case lower bound [MATH], matching the existing upper bound at fixed precision. For the bond-dependent Kitaev honeycomb family on [MATH] spins, we obtain independent lower bounds [MATH] from stabilizer nullity and [MATH] from one-qubit state preparation, established using different Hamiltonian instances. Together with an explicit LCU construction, they give the tight worst-case scaling [MATH]. As an application, we evaluate the [MATH]-count of a Hamiltonian simulation circuit based on quantum singular value transformation, with each block-encoding query compiled separately. When phase synthesis and controlled queries add at most constant-factor overhead, the simulation [MATH]-count scales as the query count times the optimal [MATH]-count per query.
tldr: Determines optimal T-gate counts for block encodings of fermionic and spin Hamiltonians using an ancilla-compression theorem and matching lower bounds.
motivation: Block encodings are central to quantum algorithms such as quantum singular value transformation and Hamiltonian simulation, so understanding their non-Clifford resource costs is important for fault-tolerant quantum computing.
method: The paper proves an ancilla-compression theorem, uses volume-covering and circuit-counting arguments for general second-quantized Hamiltonians, and derives lower bounds from stabilizer nullity and one-qubit state preparation for the Kitaev honeycomb model; upper bounds come from an explicit LCU construction.
result: It establishes tight worst-case T-count scaling for general second-quantized Hamiltonians and the bond-dependent Kitaev honeycomb family, and applies the results to QSVT-based Hamiltonian simulation, showing the simulation T-count scales as the query count times the optimal T-count per query.
conclusion: The work provides optimal T-count bounds for block encodings of structured Hamiltonians, advancing resource estimation for fault-tolerant quantum simulation.

title: Virtual Quantum Neural Networks
authors: Benchi Zhao, Xuanqiang Zhao, Yinan Li, Yingzhou Li, Giulio Chiribella
abstract: ArXiv:2609.11327v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum neural networks are a prominent model of quantum machine learning. Their training consists in the minimization of a given loss function over a parametrized family of quantum circuits, mathematically described by unitary operators, or, more generally, completely positive linear maps. In this work, we extend the notion of quantum neural network, using random sampling and classical data processing to enlarge the optimization space in a way that includes linear combinations of completely positive maps. Our extended model, called virtual quantum neural networks, leverages its enlarged optimization space to achieve increased expressivity and improved noise robustness. These benefits are illustrated in three representative tasks: quantum error mitigation, binary classification, and estimation of ground-state energies. Overall, virtual quantum neural networks offer a flexible learning paradigm that expands the space of achievable computations and strengthens the applications of near-term quantum hardware.
tldr: The paper introduces virtual quantum neural networks, an extended model that uses random sampling and classical processing to optimize over linear combinations of completely positive maps, improving expressivity and noise robustness for near-term quantum tasks.
motivation: Quantum neural networks are typically limited by the optimization space of parametrized quantum circuits or completely positive maps, which can restrict expressivity and noise resilience. The authors aim to enlarge this space without requiring additional quantum resources.
method: They define virtual quantum neural networks by combining random sampling with classical post-processing to form linear combinations of completely positive maps, effectively creating a larger optimization landscape than standard quantum neural networks.
result: The extended model demonstrates improved expressivity and noise robustness, illustrated on three tasks: quantum error mitigation, binary classification, and ground-state energy estimation.
conclusion: Virtual quantum neural networks provide a flexible learning paradigm that expands achievable computations and may strengthen applications of near-term quantum hardware, though the work remains primarily an applied quantum machine learning contribution.

title: The Quantum Overlap Gap Property And Algorithmic Hardness For The Quantum Hypergraph Max-Cut Problem
abstract: ArXiv:2609.10838v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this work, we analyze the average-case hardness of approximation for the Quantum Hypergraph Max-Cut problem using the theoretical framework of the Quantum Overlap Gap Property (QOGP). We establish two main results. Our first result applies to a wide class of stable quantum algorithms, satisfying a Lipschitz property with respect to the quantum Wasserstein distance of order [MATH]. We show a weak hardness result, demonstrating that for any Lipschitz constant [MATH], there is some [MATH] such that [MATH]-stable algorithms cannot approximate the optimal solution to Quantum Hypergraph Max-Cut on [MATH]-uniform hypergraphs in the average case. Additionally, we establish a strong hardness result where [MATH] is independent of [MATH], but only for a more restricted class of local quantum algorithms defined using the quantum Wasserstein distance of order [MATH]. We apply these results to establish concrete depth lower bounds for popular quantum algorithms for preparing near-optimal states for this problem.
tldr: The paper uses the Quantum Overlap Gap Property to prove average-case hardness and depth lower bounds for quantum algorithms approximating Quantum Hypergraph Max-Cut.
motivation: To understand the algorithmic limitations of quantum algorithms for combinatorial optimization problems and establish concrete hardness results.
method: It defines classes of stable and local quantum algorithms using the quantum Wasserstein distance and applies the Quantum Overlap Gap Property framework to derive weak and strong hardness results.
result: Weak hardness for Lipschitz-stable algorithms with arbitrary Lipschitz constant, strong hardness for local algorithms, and explicit depth lower bounds for popular quantum algorithms preparing near-optimal states.
conclusion: The work provides evidence that Quantum Hypergraph Max-Cut is hard to approximate for broad classes of quantum algorithms, contributing to quantum complexity theory.

title: Coherent Floquet Quantum Reservoirs For Molecular Property Prediction
authors: Luofei Wang, Da Zhang, Congren Wang, Yiming Li, Yuxiao Yang, Xuan Zhang, Xuefeng Cui, Zhang-Qi Yin
abstract: ArXiv:2609.11071v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum reservoir computing (QRC) uses quantum dynamics to represent input histories for prediction through a trained classical readout. Discrete time crystals (DTCs) exhibit robust subharmonic responses under periodic driving, and previous work has used their dynamics to construct DTC-QRC. Here we construct a DTC-based reservoir architecture to predict molecular properties from structural and dynamical observations. Coherent Floquet evolution processes local molecular graph events and surface-hopping frames, while controlled reset regulates the contribution of earlier inputs. Measurements at the end of each input sequence yield a feature vector of fixed dimension. Trained classical decoders use this vector for inhibitor-activity and blood--brain-barrier permeability classification and electronic-gap forecasting, while the reservoir parameters remain fixed during training. With matched input lengths and output widths, DTC-QRC outperforms echo-state networks on long-prefix graph classification and the studied ethene gap forecasting tasks. Dephasing lowers performance in both applications, consistent with a role for coherent propagation. Experiments on the Quafu superconducting quantum cloud platform show that pair observables retain task information under device noise. The architecture provides a common framework for molecular screening and time-resolved property prediction using quantum reservoir computing.
tldr: A discrete-time-crystal-based quantum reservoir computing architecture uses coherent Floquet dynamics and classical readout to predict molecular properties.
motivation: Quantum reservoir computing can represent input histories through quantum dynamics, and discrete time crystals offer robust subharmonic responses, motivating their use for molecular property prediction.
method: The authors encode molecular graph events and surface-hopping frames into coherent Floquet evolution with controlled reset, measure a fixed-dimensional feature vector, and train classical decoders while keeping reservoir parameters fixed; they also test on the Quafu superconducting cloud.
result: DTC-QRC outperforms echo-state networks on long-prefix graph classification and ethene gap forecasting, dephasing lowers performance, and pair observables retain task information under device noise.
conclusion: The work provides a common quantum reservoir computing framework for molecular screening and time-resolved property prediction, though its contribution is primarily applied quantum machine learning rather than quantum information theory.

title: Krylov Edge Spectroscopy Of Symmetry-Protected Topological Phases
abstract: ArXiv:2609.10676v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce [MATH] [MATH] [MATH], a many-body operator-space protocol for detecting and classifying one-dimensional symmetry-protected topological phases from local boundary dynamics. A Hermitian boundary operator generates a semi-infinite Krylov hopping chain whose boundary weight obeys an exact zero-frequency normalizability criterion. Open-periodic, boundary-bulk, and symmetry-preserving boundary-perturbation tests identify protected boundary memory, while a finite-depth leakage residual certifies when an explicitly reconstructed operator is already near zero frequency. Classification minimizes the normalized commutator over symmetry-resolved boundary operators in fixed charge sectors. For bosonic [MATH] phases, the recovered endpoint charge gives the cohomology label. The method requires neither many-body exact diagonalization, an explicit ground-state wavefunction or entanglement spectrum, nor a guessed dressed edge or string operator. For finite-range Hamiltonians, locality organizes the thermodynamic limit at fixed Krylov depth before the depth limit. We demonstrate the protocol in cluster, clock, Haldane, and trivial spin-1 chains. In the exactly solvable cluster chain, the transition between the gapped topological and trivial phases manifests as a localization-delocalization transition of the Krylov edge mode on the Krylov chain. This transition occurs precisely at the bulk gap closing, and its localization-length exponent coincides with the Ising correlation-length exponent. Through operator Krylov dynamics, our work turns local boundary evolution into a direct spectroscopy of many-body topology.
tldr: The paper introduces a many-body operator-space Krylov protocol that detects and classifies one-dimensional symmetry-protected topological (SPT) phases directly from local boundary dynamics.
motivation: Standard characterization of SPT phases typically relies on exact diagonalization, explicit ground-state wavefunctions, entanglement spectra, or guessed dressed edge/string operators, all of which can be costly or ad hoc; a boundary-local, operator-based diagnostic would supply a simpler and more direct spectroscopic tool.
method: A Hermitian boundary operator generates a semi-infinite Krylov hopping chain whose boundary weight obeys an exact zero-frequency normalizability criterion; open-periodic, boundary-bulk, and symmetry-preserving perturbation tests plus a symmetry-resolved commutator minimization in fixed charge sectors identify and classify protected boundary memory, as demonstrated on cluster, clock, Haldane, and trivial spin-1 chains.
result: For bosonic phases the recovered endpoint charge yields the cohomology label, and in the exactly solvable cluster chain the topological-trivial transition manifests as a localization-delocalization transition of the Krylov edge mode occurring exactly at bulk gap closing, with a localization-length exponent matching the Ising correlation-length exponent.
conclusion: Operator Krylov dynamics converts local boundary evolution into a direct spectroscopy of many-body topology, requiring neither many-body exact diagonalization, an explicit ground-state wavefunction or entanglement spectrum, nor a guessed dressed edge or string operator.

title: When Measurement Constraints Favor Quantum Computational Sensing For Stealthy Power-Grid Attack Detection
authors: Saisubramaniam Gopalakrishnan, Supreeth B S, Pranav Sarda, Ashesh Xalxo, Dagnachew Birru
abstract: ArXiv:2609.10606v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Power-grid defenses that rely on digital telemetry remain vulnerable to stealthy attacks that preserve plausible reported states while altering the underlying physical system. We study when Nitrogen-Vacancy (NV) sensing provides a useful independent physical channel, and when coherent processing before measurement adds value. Across IEEE 14-, 30-, and 118-bus simulations with Lindblad NV models, we evaluate standard FDIA, BDD-stealth, statistical-stealth, and concealed topology attacks. The results reveal an observability hierarchy: evidence shifts from digital telemetry, to reported-versus-physical consistency, to the physical NV state. Quantum Computational Sensing (QCS) follows this selectivity, becoming informative only when the physical state itself carries attack evidence. We then compare QCS, conventional 4-setting NV readout, and tomography under matched measurement budgets. At a matched total budget of only 40 physical trials per sensor on case14, QCS reaches AP [MATH], versus 0.800 for conventional NV readout and 0.751 for tomography; the same low-budget ordering holds on case30 and case118. Multi-setting methods recover as additional measurements become affordable, showing that the QCS benefit is a measurement-efficiency advantage rather than a universal accuracy advantage. Finally, we ask where the benefit varies across the three case simulations. Although the quantum-to-classical Fisher-information ratio increases from 1.21x to 1.54x, Normal--Attack Helstrom separation collapses in the harder regimes, and interleaved control substantially increases that separation only on case14, thereby quantum sensitivity does not necessarily imply task-relevant distinguishability. Our results show that realized QCS utility depends on the full chain from physical perturbation to state separation, coherent processing, and measurement under the resource constraints of the task.
tldr: The paper analyzes when NV-based quantum computational sensing improves detection of stealthy power-grid attacks over conventional readout and tomography under matched measurement budgets.
motivation: Digital telemetry defenses for power grids are vulnerable to stealthy attacks, prompting interest in independent physical channels such as NV sensing; the work asks when coherent processing before measurement adds practical value.
method: IEEE 14-, 30-, and 118-bus simulations with Lindblad NV models are used to evaluate FDIA, BDD-stealth, statistical-stealth, and concealed topology attacks, comparing QCS, conventional 4-setting NV readout, and tomography under matched budgets via Fisher information and Helstrom discrimination.
result: At 40 physical trials per sensor on case14, QCS reaches high AP versus 0.800 for conventional readout and 0.751 for tomography, but the advantage is measurement efficiency, not universal accuracy; quantum Fisher-information gains do not guarantee task-relevant distinguishability as Helstrom separation collapses in harder regimes.
conclusion: Realized QCS utility depends on the full chain from physical perturbation to state separation, coherent processing, and measurement under task resource constraints.

title: A Quantum-Inspired Dequantization Method For Diagonally Weighted Matrix Functions: Application To Learning With Optimized Random Features
authors: Natsuto Isogai, Mio Murao, Hayata Yamasaki
abstract: ArXiv:2609.10729v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum-inspired classical algorithms have dequantized several quantum machine learning routines by replacing quantum linear-algebra subroutines with classical counterparts. However, the sampler based on quantum singular value transformation (QSVT) for learning with optimized random features is not covered by existing dequantization frameworks, because the matrix to be inverted is not itself available through sampling access. In this work, we develop a classical algorithm to address this type of quantum-advantage candidate. Our method samples heavy indices, reduces the transformation to a small principal block, and outputs a sparse classical representation with operator-norm guarantees. Applying this method dequantizes the sampler for optimized random features, giving a classical sampler with prescribed accuracy and polynomially related runtime. These results show that the factorization underlying a quantum block encoding can itself provide sufficient classical structure even when sampling-and-query access to the composite matrix is unavailable.
tldr: A classical dequantization algorithm for a QSVT-based sampler used in learning with optimized random features.
motivation: Existing dequantization frameworks do not cover the QSVT sampler because the matrix to be inverted is not directly available through sampling access.
method: The authors sample heavy indices, reduce the transformation to a small principal block, and output a sparse classical representation with operator-norm guarantees.
result: Applying the method dequantizes the sampler for optimized random features, giving a classical sampler with prescribed accuracy and polynomially related runtime.
conclusion: The factorization underlying a quantum block encoding can itself provide sufficient classical structure even when sampling-and-query access to the composite matrix is unavailable.

title: Tight Time-Space Lower Bounds For Collision Finding And Element Distinctness Under Label Symmetry
abstract: ArXiv:2609.10808v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: How much memory is needed to retain the quantum speedup for collision finding? For a uniformly random function [MATH], the BHT algorithm finds a collision using [MATH] queries and a quantumly accessible classical table containing [MATH] input-output pairs, whereas a logarithmic-space Grover search uses [MATH] queries. Determining the optimal query-space tradeoff between these extremes remains a major open problem. We resolve this equation within the class of label-symmetric algorithms, which treat the function [MATH]'s output labels as interchangeable. We prove that such algorithm that makes [MATH] queries, uses [MATH] qubits, and finds a collision in a uniformly random function [MATH] with constant probability satisfies $[MATH][MATH]M=N[MATH]f: [n] \to [n^2][MATH][MATH][MATH]S[MATH]O(S/\log N)$ collision-free database entries. Substituting this estimate into the compressed oracle technique yields the stated tradeoffs.
tldr: The paper proves tight time-space lower bounds for quantum collision finding and element distinctness within the class of label-symmetric algorithms.
motivation: Determining the optimal query-space tradeoff for quantum collision finding, between the BHT algorithm and logarithmic-space Grover search, remains a major open problem.
method: It restricts to label-symmetric algorithms that treat output labels as interchangeable, and combines this symmetry with the compressed oracle technique to bound the number of collision-free database entries.
result: For label-symmetric algorithms making a certain number of queries, using a certain number of qubits, and succeeding with constant probability, the number of collision-free database entries is O(S / log N), which yields stated tight tradeoffs for collision finding and element distinctness.
conclusion: The work resolves the query-space tradeoff within the label-symmetric class, though the general case without label symmetry remains open.

title: Physics Of Information Geometry - Part Ii: Small-Step Active Inference On The Probability Simplex
abstract: ArXiv:2609.11187v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper is the second in a two-part investigation of the physics of information geometry. While Part I develops a physical foundation for distributional motion on the probability simplex, the present paper studies how that framework manifests in active inference. The treatment is fully self-contained and does not require familiarity with Part I. We focus in particular on active inference through small distributional steps and the geometric structure induced by such local motion. Starting from an initial distribution, an agent evolves its belief state toward a final target distribution through a sequence of constrained updates. We define a relative free energy functional with respect to the preferred distribution and extend it to a relative potential energy analogous to the Helmholtz/Gibbs free-energy decomposition. The evolution is subject to a per-step kinetic constraint expressed through the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence between consecutive distributions, which serves as a discrete kinetic energy on the probability simplex. Using the information-geometric Pythagorean theorem on KL balls, we show that sufficiently small local moves dominate large direct jumps, and that greedy maximization of free-energy reduction is globally optimal under the kinetic constraint. This leads to a sequential variational principle in which the optimal trajectory minimizes the associated Lagrangian of the optimization problem. Similar to classical mechanics, the Lagrangian takes on the form as the difference between the kinetic and potential terms, establishing a least-action principle for distributional motion on the simplex. The resulting optimal update admits a closed form as an exponentially tilted version of the current distribution toward the preferred distribution, parametrized by an inverse-temperature-like multiplier. We further extend the framework to incorporate state-dependent geodesic...
tldr: A theoretical study of active inference via small distributional steps on the probability simplex, using information geometry and a thermodynamic least-action formalism.
motivation: To establish a physical foundation for distributional motion and optimal belief updates in active inference, extending a geometric framework from Part I.
method: Defines a relative free energy and a Kullback-Leibler kinetic constraint, then applies the information-geometric Pythagorean theorem to derive a sequential variational principle and a closed-form exponentially tilted update.
result: Shows that sufficiently small local moves dominate large jumps and that greedy free-energy reduction is globally optimal under the kinetic constraint; the optimal trajectory minimizes a Lagrangian of kinetic minus potential terms with an inverse-temperature multiplier.
conclusion: Provides a least-action principle for distributional motion on the probability simplex and extends the framework to state-dependent geodesics.

title: Data Protection In Function-Correcting Symbol-Pair Codes: Redundancy Bounds And Protection Profiles
abstract: ArXiv:2609.10989v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In several storage systems, including DNA storage and flash memory, errors affect neighbouring symbols jointly, and the Hamming metric does not adequately capture such error patterns. The symbol-pair read channel, introduced by Cassuto and Blaum~, addresses this by reading consecutive pairs of symbols rather than individual symbols. Motivated by this, we introduce function-correcting symbol-pair codes with data protection (FCSPC-DP), which guarantee reliable recovery of a desired function of the message while simultaneously protecting the message itself against symbol-pair errors. We derive bounds on the optimal redundancy of such codes and establish a relationship with joint-pair distance matrices. We also give explicit constructions of FCSPC-DP for locally pair-bounded functions and symbol-pair weight functions. We introduce the pair-separation constant of a function, the minimum symbol-pair distance between messages sharing a function value, and show that when it is sufficiently large, data protection requires no additional redundancy: the optimal redundancy coincides with that of the corresponding code without data protection. Considering the symbol-pair analogue of the [MATH]-distance graph, we introduce two code invariants, the generation profile and the disconnection threshold, and use them to characterise a code's protection properties. Relating the two metrics through these invariants yields upper and lower bounds on the symbol-pair threshold in terms of its Hamming counterpart, both of which are attained. We further extend the classical Plotkin and sphere-packing bounds to this setting.
tldr: The paper introduces function-correcting symbol-pair codes with data protection (FCSPC-DP), deriving redundancy bounds and protection-profile invariants for codes that simultaneously recover a function of the message and protect the message against symbol-pair errors.
motivation: Storage systems such as DNA storage and flash memory suffer from errors that jointly affect neighbouring symbols, which the Hamming metric fails to capture, motivating coding schemes based on the symbol-pair read channel.
method: The authors define FCSPC-DP, derive lower bounds on optimal redundancy, relate them to joint-pair distance matrices, and introduce the pair-separation constant, generation profile, and disconnection threshold to characterise protection properties.
result: They show that when the pair-separation constant is sufficiently large, data protection requires no extra redundancy, and they extend the Plotkin and sphere-packing bounds while giving upper and lower bounds on the symbol-pair threshold in terms of its Hamming counterpart.
conclusion: The work extends classical function-correcting code theory to the symbol-pair setting, providing new bounds, invariants, and constructions relevant to storage channels with correlated symbol errors.

title: Maximal Kolmogorov Complexity In A Hamming Ball
abstract: ArXiv:2609.11362v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The minimal Kolmogorov complexity of a string within Hamming distance r of a given string x is the algorithmic rate-distortion function of x, and Vereshchagin and Vitanyi characterized completely which shapes it can have. This paper is about the opposite extreme. For a binary string x of length n let g_x(r) denote the maximal Kolmogorov complexity of a string within Hamming distance r of x; we study which values, and more generally which functions of r, this quantity can attain. First we characterize, up to an additive error O(log n), the possible values of the triple (C(x),r,g_x(r)): writing r_k for the radius of a Hamming ball of cardinality about 2^k, a triple (k,r,l) is realizable if and only if log V(r_k + r) < l < min{n, k+log V(r)}, where V(a) is the cardinality of a ball of radius a. In particular, for r_k+r > n/2 both bounds collapse to n and only l = n is realizable. The two ends of this interval correspond to the two extreme ways of placing a set of complexity k in the cube: a single Hamming ball, where the lower bound comes from Harper's isoperimetric inequality, and an error-correcting code, which for the intermediate parameters we relax to a family of centers with bounded covering multiplicity, in the spirit of list decoding. Then we turn to the function r -> g_x(r) as a whole: we establish four properties that it always has, and show that the minimal and the maximal functions consistent with these properties are both attained, for every complexity level k. Which intermediate profiles are attainable remains open.
tldr: Characterizes the maximal Kolmogorov complexity within a Hamming ball, linking it to isoperimetric inequalities and list decoding.
motivation: The minimal complexity within a Hamming ball (algorithmic rate-distortion) was fully characterized; this paper studies the opposite extreme, the maximal complexity, to understand the algorithmic structure of Hamming balls.
method: Uses Kolmogorov complexity, Hamming ball combinatorics, Harper's isoperimetric inequality, and error-correcting codes/list decoding to derive bounds on the triple (C(x), r, g_x(r)) and properties of the function g_x(r).
result: A triple (k, r, l) is realizable iff log V(r_k+r) < l < min{n, k+log V(r)} up to O(log n); for r_k+r > n/2 only l = n is realizable; four properties of g_x(r) are established, with the minimal and maximal functions consistent with them attained, leaving intermediate profiles open.
conclusion: This work advances classical algorithmic information theory and coding theory, but has no direct quantum information content or immediate relevance to quantum research directions.

title: A Machine-checked Proof Of The Dong-Yang Classification Of Optimal (n,4) Binary Codes For BSCs
abstract: ArXiv:2609.10579v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a machine-checked Lean~4 formalization of Dong and Yang's classification of optimal finite-length [MATH] binary block codes for binary symmetric channels. The formalization was developed mainly by feeding the paper's proofs to an AI tool. To establish correctness, the authors verified the main theorem statements in Lean and the accepted axioms.
