Independently of that asymptotic argument, we develop a new analysis based on the log-volume of the polar MinCE as a potential function. We prove its convexity with an explicit gradient formula and establish global linear contraction of the potential gap along each trajectory. The contraction factor is existential and instance-dependent. This gives both a separate convergence proof and a finite volume-ratio iteration bound. We further analyze an inexact polarity process in which each MinCE subproblem is solved only approximately, and derive sufficient oracle tolerances for producing a prescribed volume approximation. Combining this outer analysis with existing algorithms for MinCE gives conditional arithmetic estimates based on the path-following Newton method, the barycentric coordinate descent, and the away-step Frank-Wolfe method. Numerical experiments compare these oracle choices with two MaxIE baselines and illustrate that performance depends on matching the MinCE solver to the instance geometry.
tldr: A geometric polarity-based iteration for the maximum-volume inscribed ellipsoid (MaxIE) problem in polytopes, with a new log-volume potential analysis giving linear contraction and finite iteration bounds.
motivation: Prior work on the Khachiyan–Todd polarity process for MaxIE only established asymptotic convergence and lacked a volume-ratio rate, so the authors seek both a rigorous rate and a practical inexact-oracle analysis.
method: The process shifts the polar polytope about an interior point, solves a minimum-volume covering ellipsoid (MinCE) subproblem, and polarizes back; convergence is analyzed via the log-volume of the polar MinCE as a convex potential with an explicit gradient and oracle-tolerance bounds for inexact solves.
result: The authors prove global linear contraction of the potential gap with an instance-dependent factor, obtain a finite volume-ratio iteration bound, and give conditional arithmetic complexity estimates combined with path-following Newton, barycentric coordinate descent, and away-step Frank–Wolfe solvers.
conclusion: The paper supplies a new convergence proof and complexity analysis for polarity-based MaxIE, with numerics showing that performance depends on matching the MinCE solver to the polytope geometry.

title: Online Change-Point Monitoring For Object-valued Time Series
authors: Yi Zhang, Tim Kutta, Xiaofeng Shao
abstract: ArXiv:2609.10889v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop closed- and open-end procedures for monitoring changes in the marginal distribution of object-valued time series. The method combines two distance-based Hilbert-space embeddings, a monitoring-time-dependent projection, and self-normalization. It is computable entirely from pairwise distances, does not require long-run variance estimation, and admits exact recursive updates. Under weak temporal dependence, the closed-end null limit is a pivotal Brownian functional. For monitoring over an unbounded horizon, we introduce a growing monitoring-time weight, establish a maximal inequality and uniform remote-tail control, and derive an open-end pivotal limit together with an equivalent fixed-interval representation for critical-value simulation. Both procedures are consistent against fixed marginal changes and retain the [MATH] and [MATH] local detection boundaries associated with the linear and quadratic projection signals. Simulations with distribution-valued time series illustrate favorable numerical properties, and an application to monthly stock-return distributions illustrates the usefulness of our procedure. Further simulations with graph-valued time series and an application to spatial point processes of seismic activity are reported in the supplementary material.
tldr: The paper develops online change-point monitoring procedures for object-valued time series using distance-based Hilbert-space embeddings, self-normalization, and projection techniques.
motivation: Monitoring distributional changes in complex object-valued time series is challenging because standard methods require long-run variance estimation and are not directly applicable to non-Euclidean data.
method: It combines two distance-based Hilbert-space embeddings, a monitoring-time-dependent projection, and self-normalization, yielding closed- and open-end procedures with exact recursive updates and pivotal limit distributions.
result: The procedures are consistent against fixed marginal changes, achieve established local detection boundaries, and show favorable performance in simulations and applications to stock-return distributions, graph-valued series, and seismic point processes.
conclusion: The proposed framework provides a practical and theoretically grounded approach for online monitoring of object-valued time series without long-run variance estimation.

title: Typical Dynamical Properties Of Operators On $\ell_p$
abstract: ArXiv:2609.10957v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate the typical dynamical properties of hypercyclic operators in [MATH], the set of all bounded linear operators on [MATH] whose norms are at most [MATH], when [MATH], [MATH]. We show that, with respect to SOT[MATH], a typical operator [MATH] is weakly mixing, is weakly disjoint from a given hypercyclic operator [MATH], is not topologically ergodic, and satisfies [MATH] is disjoint hypercyclic for any [MATH]. We also study the typical dynamical properties for the concrete family [MATH], endowed with the norm topology, where [MATH] is a bilateral weighted backward shift.
tldr: The paper studies typical dynamical properties of hypercyclic operators on ℓ_p spaces under the strong operator topology and norm topology.
motivation: To understand generic dynamical behavior, including weak mixing and disjoint hypercyclicity, of bounded linear operators on ℓ_p spaces.
method: It uses Baire category arguments in the strong operator topology and analyzes a concrete family of bilateral weighted backward shifts under the norm topology.
result: A typical operator is shown to be weakly mixing, weakly disjoint from a given hypercyclic operator, not topologically ergodic, and disjoint hypercyclic with its powers.
conclusion: The work characterizes typical operator dynamics on ℓ_p but has no clear connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: A Second-Order Method For Locating Critical Points Of Prescribed Index On Energy Landscapes
abstract: ArXiv:2609.11038v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Exploring high dimensional energy landscape is a challenging problem in many applications where both ground states and transition states offer important information about the underlying physical systems. To facilitate the computational exploration, we propose a cubic-regularized second-order method for locating critical points of prescribed index, including both energy minima (with an index [MATH]) and transition states (saddle points with positive index). At each step of the iteration, the proposed method involves several ingredients, such as updating the eigen-directions of the Hessian according to the prescribed index, reflecting the gradient and the Hessian along selected unstable eigen-directions, if any, and constructing the next step by solving a cubic-regularized subproblem. Under suitable assumptions, we show that, when the eigenspace and the cubic subproblem are solved exactly, the iteration converges locally and quadratically to a critical point of the prescribed index. We further establish convergence results in the inexact setting, where both the eigenspace computation and the solution of the cubic subproblem are performed approximately. We show that the resulting iteration retains local linear convergence, with the convergence rate depending on the accuracy of the inexact computations. Moreover, we prove that the fixed points of the algorithm are precisely critical points of the prescribed index. In addition, we introduce an adaptive strategy for updating the cubic regularization parameter to improve robustness and computational efficiency of the proposed algorithm. Numerical experiments confirm the predicted convergence behavior, demonstrate the effectiveness of the adaptive strategy, and illustrate the capability of the proposed method for locating critical points and constructing solution landscapes.
tldr: A cubic-regularized second-order method is proposed for locating critical points of prescribed index, including minima and saddle points, on high-dimensional energy landscapes.
motivation: Exploring energy landscapes for ground states and transition states is challenging, and efficient computational methods are needed.
method: The algorithm updates Hessian eigen-directions according to the prescribed index, reflects gradient and Hessian along unstable directions, and solves a cubic-regularized subproblem, with adaptive regularization and inexact variants.
result: Local quadratic convergence is proven for exact subproblems and local linear convergence for inexact computations, with fixed points corresponding to critical points of the prescribed index; numerical experiments validate the approach.
conclusion: The method effectively locates critical points of a given index and can assist in constructing solution landscapes.

title: Who Pays For A Connected Public Good?
abstract: ArXiv:2609.10565v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Connectivity can turn separate contributions into a public good that benefits participants and nonparticipants alike. Yet only participants pay for it, and each can avoid her charge by withdrawing while enjoying whatever public output survives. How do network connections constrain who can or must pay, and how large a cost can the group bear? We study a participation game in which public output equals the size of the largest connected group of active players, whose members divide a fixed operating cost. The output a participant destroys by withdrawing is her withdrawal responsibility and bounds her payment. These bounds determine the group's cost-bearing capacity and, whenever the group can be kept active, which participants must pay. We prove that among connected networks with at least five players, the path uniquely maximizes the cost-bearing capacity of a group, yet minimizes the expected surviving output after a uniformly selected participant withdraws. As the group grows, the ratio of maximal capacity to gross social benefit under full participation converges to one quarter. Fragility can therefore strengthen voluntary finance, but even the most financeable network cannot close the gap between the value it creates and what its participants will pay to sustain it.
tldr: This paper studies a classical participation game on networks where public output equals the size of the largest connected active group, and analyzes who must pay and how much cost a group can bear.
motivation: Connectivity can create a public good shared by participants and nonparticipants, but only participants pay, and each can withdraw to avoid charges while still benefiting from surviving output. The paper asks how network structure constrains cost-bearing and participation.
method: The authors formulate a participation game in which output is the size of the largest connected active component and members divide a fixed operating cost, then analyze withdrawal responsibility bounds and prove extremal properties among connected networks.
result: Among connected networks with at least five players, the path uniquely maximizes cost-bearing capacity while minimizing expected surviving output after a uniformly random withdrawal; the maximal capacity-to-gross-benefit ratio converges to one quarter as group size grows.
conclusion: Fragility can strengthen voluntary finance, but even the most financeable network cannot fully close the gap between the value it creates and what participants are willing to pay to sustain it.

title: Threshold Choice, Not Sample Size, Bounds Trustless Verification Of Nondeterministic Compound Ai Workflows
abstract: ArXiv:2609.10601v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Compound AI pipelines chain LLM calls, retrievers, and tools and are nondeterministic: sampling, model updates, and volatile tool responses make one input yield different outputs across runs. Such pipelines increasingly run across edge, cloud, and orbital nodes owned by no single party, whose optimizations discard intermediate results before inspection. Verifying reproduction there means tolerating nondeterministic outputs, a node that may not report honestly, and intermittent access to any shared record; existing work addresses at most two at once. We give a protocol covering all three: it commits digests of each stage's inputs, outputs, and context under a policy digest pinning the metric and threshold, anchors them without trusting the executing node, defers under partition, and decides a challenge on the median of [MATH] re-executions, with no quorum. Where that procedure breaks is the main result. On a synthetic HotpotQA pipeline a calibrated fixed threshold accepts 44 of 45 honest reproductions and rejects 104 of 105 divergent pairs, yet lets same-input fabrication through in 27 of 29 trials at k=5, more samples being no help since sampling sharpens an estimate without moving it. Holding that metric and this pipeline's re-execution spread fixed, the binding constraint is the threshold rather than the sample size: one derived per execution detects 19 of 29 where the best constant matched to the same zero honest rejections reaches 9, rejects no honest commitment at k=5 though 3 of 15 at k=3, and catches 11 of 15 of an attacker built against it, which has to aim at a target drawn only after its commitment exists. That rule is measured rather than deployed.
tldr: The paper studies trustless verification of nondeterministic compound AI workflows and argues that the decision threshold, not sample size, is the binding constraint.
motivation: Compound AI pipelines are nondeterministic and increasingly run across mixed-trust infrastructure, making reproduction verification difficult under intermittent access and potentially dishonest nodes.
method: The authors propose a protocol that commits stage input/output/context digests under a policy digest, anchors them without trusting the executing node, defers under partition, and decides challenges by re-execution medians without quorum.
result: On a synthetic HotpotQA pipeline, a calibrated fixed threshold accepts most honest reproductions and rejects most divergent pairs, but still allows same-input fabrication at k=5; a per-execution derived threshold detects more attacks without rejecting honest commitments.
conclusion: For this pipeline and metric, threshold choice is the dominant verification constraint rather than sample size, though the proposed rule is measured rather than deployed.

title: Feasible Disjunction For Random Resolution
abstract: ArXiv:2609.10602v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We show that a (stronger) version of random resolution has the feasible disjunction property. This is the first instance of a proof system not known to have feasible interpolation, which nevertheless has the feasible disjunction property.
tldr: The paper proves that a stronger version of the random resolution proof system has the feasible disjunction property, marking the first such system not known to have feasible interpolation.
motivation: Feasible interpolation and feasible disjunction are important properties in proof complexity that relate propositional proof systems to computational complexity. The work aims to separate these properties by exhibiting a proof system with one but not known to have the other.
method: The author introduces a stronger variant of the random resolution proof system and gives a proof-theoretic argument establishing the feasible disjunction property for it.
result: The stronger random resolution system is shown to have the feasible disjunction property, while it is not known to possess feasible interpolation.
conclusion: This provides the first instance of a proof system with feasible disjunction but without known feasible interpolation, contributing to the understanding of proof-complexity properties.

title: Black-Box Membership Inference Via Word-Level Probability Estimation
authors: Shengjie Niu, Yeheng Ge, Jian Huang
abstract: ArXiv:2609.10611v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Membership inference attacks (MIAs) have emerged as critical tools for auditing privacy risks in large language models (LLMs), aiming to determine whether a given text was included in a model's training corpus. However, most existing MIAs require access to per-token logits or probabilities, making them inapplicable in practice to proprietary LLMs that expose only textual continuations. To address this underexplored setting, we propose Word-level Probability MIA (WPMIA), a statistically principled MIA for strict black-box privacy auditing. WPMIA estimates word-level generation probabilities via Monte Carlo sampling with local kernel smoothing, then aggregates these estimates into a sequence-level likelihood estimator. Furthermore, WPMIA constructs the likelihood conditioned on different prefixes, thereby amplifying the distributional differences between members and non-members. We evaluate WPMIA across various open-source LLMs and find that it consistently outperforms existing black-box baselines. Importantly, we also evaluate WPMIA on modern proprietary LLMs, including GPT-5-Chat, Gemini-2.5-Flash, and Claude-4.5-Haiku, achieving an average TPR@5\%FPR of 42.0 across these models. These results offer a sound foundation for future research on strict black-box membership inference. Code is available at {[URL].
tldr: The paper proposes a word-level probability membership inference attack (WPMIA) for strict black-box privacy auditing of large language models.
motivation: Existing membership inference attacks typically require access to per-token logits or probabilities, which are unavailable for proprietary LLMs that only expose textual continuations.
method: WPMIA estimates word-level generation probabilities via Monte Carlo sampling with local kernel smoothing, aggregates them into a sequence-level likelihood estimator, and conditions on different prefixes to amplify member/non-member differences.
result: WPMIA consistently outperforms existing black-box baselines on open-source LLMs and achieves an average TPR@5%FPR of 42.0 on proprietary models including GPT-5-Chat, Gemini-2.5-Flash, and Claude-4.5-Haiku.
conclusion: The method offers a statistically principled foundation for strict black-box membership inference and privacy auditing of LLMs.

title: Understanding In-Context Multimodal Jailbreaks Via Posterior Reweighting
authors: Xu Zhang, Dev Mistry, Xiang Xu, Ren Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2609.10613v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In-context learning (ICL) jailbreaks reveal a critical vulnerability in multimodal large language models (MLLMs): harmful demonstrations in the prompt can induce unsafe outputs without modifying model parameters. Despite extensive empirical evidence, existing work lacks a principled understanding of why such jailbreaks reliably succeed or how their effectiveness scales with context composition. We propose a posterior reweighting framework that models a safety-aligned MLLM as implicitly operating over competing behavioral modes, and interprets in-context demonstrations as inference-time evidence that dynamically shifts the model's posterior preference between safe and harmful behaviors. This view formalizes jailbreak as a process of evidence accumulation, yielding predictive scaling laws with respect to demonstration count, harmful ratio, adversarial strength, and semantic diversity. Guided by this framework, we introduce a posterior-aware inference-time defense that adaptively injects benign counter-evidence based on estimated risk, effectively suppressing harmful posterior drift while preserving model utility. Compared to existing in-context defenses, our method achieves a significantly improved robustness-utility trade-off under a fixed intervention budget. Together, our results establish posterior reweighting as a unifying and predictive framework for understanding and mitigating ICL jailbreak in MLLMs.
tldr: The paper proposes a posterior reweighting framework to understand and defend against in-context multimodal jailbreaks in safety-aligned multimodal large language models.
motivation: In-context learning jailbreaks expose a critical vulnerability in multimodal LLMs, but existing work lacks a principled explanation for why harmful demonstrations reliably succeed and how their effectiveness scales with context composition.
method: The authors model a safety-aligned MLLM as operating over competing behavioral modes and interpret in-context demonstrations as inference-time evidence that dynamically shifts the posterior preference between safe and harmful behaviors, yielding predictive scaling laws and a posterior-aware defense.
result: The framework predicts jailbreak scaling with demonstration count, harmful ratio, adversarial strength, and semantic diversity; the proposed defense improves the robustness-utility trade-off under a fixed intervention budget compared to existing in-context defenses.
conclusion: Posterior reweighting is presented as a unifying and predictive framework for understanding and mitigating ICL jailbreaks in multimodal LLMs.

title: Architecting The Secure Ai-soc: A Neurosymbolic Framework For Pipeline Integrity And Threat Mitigation
authors: Anna Gazani, Spyridon Kounoupidis, Panagiotis Katsaros, Nikolaos Kekatos, Grigorios Tsoumakas, Georgios Koutidis
abstract: ArXiv:2609.10707v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) into Security Operations Centers (SOCs) streamlines threat intelligence but introduces critical vulnerabilities, notably indirect prompt injection via log poisoning. Adversaries exploit this vector to execute multistep ``promptware'' kill chains by embedding malicious payloads within system logs to hijack the LLM's operational logic. Securing this pipeline presents a dichotomy: deterministic defenses are computationally efficient yet semantically blind, while purely neural evaluations introduce prohibitive latency and probabilistic flaws. To address this, we propose a novel neurosymbolic defense-in-depth architecture that ensures end-to-end pipeline integrity. The primary layer employs customized SIEM decoders as a deterministic pre-filter, performing immediate structural sanitization to neutralize volumetric padding and signature-based injections at the ingestion edge. The secondary layer leverages NeMo Guardrails to enforce strict semantic boundaries through self-checking validation on the structured SIEM alerts prior to LLM processing. Furthermore, the framework integrates a closed-loop telemetry system, providing critical Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) visibility into thwarted attacks directly within the SOC dashboard. We present a comprehensive experimental evaluation mapped to the MITRE ATLAS taxonomy, assessing the framework against diverse prompt injections. Our results demonstrate that this synergistic approach effectively dismantles the promptware kill chain - bounding LLM stochasticity with verifiable constraints, and delivering a resilient, highly observable defense mechanism for next-generation AI-SOCs.
tldr: The paper proposes a neurosymbolic defense-in-depth architecture to secure LLM-integrated Security Operations Centers against indirect prompt injection and promptware kill chains.
motivation: Integrating LLMs into SOCs improves threat intelligence but introduces vulnerabilities like log poisoning and multistep promptware attacks, while existing deterministic and purely neural defenses each suffer from semantic blindness or latency and probabilistic flaws.
method: The framework combines customized SIEM decoders as a deterministic pre-filter for structural sanitization with NeMo Guardrails for semantic self-checking validation, plus closed-loop telemetry for human-in-the-loop visibility.
result: Experimental evaluation mapped to MITRE ATLAS shows the approach dismantles the promptware kill chain, bounding LLM stochasticity with verifiable constraints and improving resilience and observability.
conclusion: The neurosymbolic architecture provides a resilient, observable defense mechanism for next-generation AI-SOCs, though it lies outside the quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, and hybrid systems focus areas.

title: Temporal And Multimodal Deep Learning For Cyberattack Detection In Leo Satellite Systems
authors: Kyle Stein, Guillermo Francia III, Eman El-Sheikh, Hossain Shahriar
abstract: ArXiv:2609.10746v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The growing reliance on Low-Earth Orbit (LEO) satellite communication systems has increased the need for intelligent methods capable of detecting cyberattacks across complex and dynamic space environments. Unlike conventional network intrusion detection, satellite systems generate heterogeneous information across radio-frequency (RF) links, onboard hardware, and orbital operations. However, many existing approaches either rely on terrestrial intrusion datasets or evaluate individual observations independently, limiting their ability to capture temporal attack behavior specific to LEO satellites. In this work, we conduct a systematic study of deep-learning-based cyberattack detection using the recently introduced satellite-specific UNSW-IoTSAT dataset. We investigate structured learning architectures that preserve hardware, orbital, and RF information, including a Subsystem-Fusion MLP and a hierarchical multimodal Transformer that models both cross-subsystem interactions and temporal evolution. We further evaluate leakage-resistant row-level and temporal settings, along with cross-satellite generalization, to characterize how model architecture and evaluation protocol influence satellite cyberattack detection. Experimental results demonstrate the value of structured multimodal modeling and rigorous evaluation, with the hierarchical Transformer achieving up to 91.66% accuracy and 85.63% macro F1 under the leakage-resistant evaluation protocol.
tldr: This paper studies deep-learning architectures for cyberattack detection in LEO satellite systems using the UNSW-IoTSAT dataset.
motivation: Growing reliance on LEO satellite communication increases the need for intelligent intrusion detection that captures temporal and multimodal attack behavior specific to satellite environments.
method: The authors evaluate structured learning architectures including a Subsystem-Fusion MLP and a hierarchical multimodal Transformer that models cross-subsystem interactions and temporal evolution under leakage-resistant evaluation protocols.
result: The hierarchical Transformer achieves up to 91.66% accuracy and 85.63% macro F1 under a leakage-resistant evaluation protocol.
conclusion: Structured multimodal modeling and rigorous evaluation protocols improve satellite cyberattack detection and cross-satellite generalization.

title: Big Enough To Break Out: Tracking The Rising Capability Of Llm Penetration-Testing Agents
authors: Victoria Lovelace, Cameron Berryman, Yuhan You, Suhas Reddy Adavelly, Joel Sadler, Daniel Graham
abstract: ArXiv:2609.10780v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly applied to penetration testing, but we still know little about what they can do or how they fail. We compare two PentestGPT-based systems: a legacy human-in-the-loop system running the open-weight Kimi K2.5, and a newer autonomous system running Claude Opus 4.8. Across three public targets, the autonomous system solves all three, including the two the legacy system never finishes. The legacy result is the more surprising of the two. Even on the machines the legacy system fails to solve, it completes about half the subtasks, while running on ordinary university GPUs with no provider guardrails. We can describe the trend but not explain it, since model, harness, autonomy, and memory architecture all change together. Its direction still points to the next question: what will limit these agents as they take on more complex tasks? The usual answer is long-horizon memory, the loss of access to earlier findings during long attack chains. We test it by adding a coverage-memory layer to both systems, and neither improves outcomes. In the legacy stalled runs we could review, the limiting factor appeared to be planning and commitment rather than lost memory: agents held the evidence for a route forward and never turned it into a concrete exploitation hypothesis, which may suggest that offensive capability will advance with agents' ability to plan rather than with better memory. The same subtask scoring that tracks this capability is available to defenders, who can measure it as it rises instead of waiting to meet it in the field.
tldr: This paper compares two PentestGPT-based LLM agents on penetration-testing tasks and finds that autonomous Claude Opus 4.8 solves all three test targets while a legacy Kimi K2.5 human-in-the-loop system fails, with planning rather than memory appearing to limit the legacy agent.
motivation: LLM agents are increasingly used for penetration testing, but their capabilities and failure modes are poorly understood, motivating a direct comparison of two systems.
method: The authors compare a legacy human-in-the-loop PentestGPT system running Kimi K2.5 against a newer autonomous system running Claude Opus 4.8 across three public targets, then add a coverage-memory layer to test whether long-horizon memory is the limiting factor.
result: The autonomous system solves all three targets, while the legacy system fails to finish two but still completes about half the subtasks; adding coverage-memory does not improve outcomes for either system.
conclusion: The limiting factor for the legacy stalled runs appears to be planning and commitment rather than memory loss, suggesting offensive agent capability may advance more through better planning than better memory, and the same subtask scoring can help defenders track capability growth.

title: DriftNet: A Dual-Head Trajectory Transformer For Detecting And Localizing Prompt Injection In Llm Agents
abstract: ArXiv:2609.10892v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When an indirect prompt injection succeeds against an LLM agent, the compromise is visible in the agent's own behavior: a benign prefix of tool calls, a poisoned observation, and a suffix of actions that serve the attacker. An operator needs three facts: where the attack entered, which steps it corrupted, and whether apparent poison was resisted. Existing systems return either a whole-trace verdict or a single unsafe index. We present DriftNet, a dual-head trajectory Transformer that reads a logged tool-call trajectory and answers all three questions in one forward pass: one head classifies the trajectory as compromised or not, and a second assigns every step one of four labels (benign, injection point, hijacked, failed injection). To our knowledge it is the first supervised detector to produce this joint output. A frozen sentence encoder and four identity-free world features embed each step; the trained trunk, under two million parameters and optimized with a class-weighted joint objective over both heads, needs no access to the agent's model. On the task-disjoint split of the AgentDrift benchmark (12,536 trajectories, 71,024 labeled steps), with a 20-configuration sweep bounding hyperparameter sensitivity to 0.011 F1 and the test part evaluated exactly once, DriftNet reaches trajectory-level F1 of 0.983, exact injection-point recovery on 98.7% of attacked trajectories, hijacked-span IoU of 0.979, zero flags on 218 resisted attacks, and 2.9% flags on hard negatives. A surface baseline retrained on the identical split recovers 11.1% of partial hijacks and 17.1% of delayed executions; DriftNet reaches 98.6% and 93.2% while lowering every false-alarm rate. Reading all 26 residual errors shows that most misses trace to trajectories whose labeled injection observation carries no legible instruction, and we report the benchmark's measured world-identity regularity alongside the results.
tldr: DriftNet is a dual-head trajectory Transformer that detects and localizes prompt injection in LLM agent tool-call logs, jointly classifying compromise and labeling each step.
motivation: Indirect prompt injection in LLM agents requires operators to know where an attack entered, which steps it corrupted, and whether poison was resisted, but existing systems return only whole-trace verdicts or single unsafe indices.
method: The model embeds each step using a frozen sentence encoder and four identity-free world features, then a sub-2M-parameter trunk with two heads is trained with a class-weighted joint objective to output a trajectory-level label and per-step labels without access to the agent's model.
result: On the AgentDrift benchmark, DriftNet achieves trajectory-level F1 0.983, 98.7% exact injection-point recovery, 0.979 hijacked-span IoU, zero flags on 218 resisted attacks, and 2.9% flags on hard negatives, greatly outperforming a surface baseline.
conclusion: The authors present the first supervised detector for joint trajectory-level compromise classification and per-step injection localization, with low hyperparameter sensitivity and interpretable error analysis.

title: Empirical Evaluation Of Data Poisoning Attacks In Supervised Learning
authors: Muhammad Abusaqer Toshif Khan (minot State University)
abstract: ArXiv:2609.10952v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Data poisoning corrupts training data to degrade a model or to plant attacker-controlled behavior. This study evaluates two representative training-time attacks, label flipping and backdoor poisoning, on MNIST and Fashion-MNIST with three baseline classifiers: Logistic Regression, Linear SVM, and Random Forest. Clean training is compared with poisoning rates of 5%, 10%, and 20% using clean-test accuracy, macro-precision, macro-recall, macro-F1, and, for backdoors, attack success rate. Label flipping caused clear degradation, largest for Logistic Regression and Linear SVM, while Random Forest stayed comparatively stable. Backdoor poisoning reached attack success rates from 0.9667 to 1.0000 on both datasets and all three models while often keeping clean-test performance near baseline. The results separate indiscriminate poisoning, which shows up in standard metrics, from targeted backdoor poisoning, which stays comparatively stealthy while embedding highly effective malicious behavior, and they support security-oriented evaluation beyond conventional clean-test metrics.
tldr: This paper empirically evaluates label flipping and backdoor poisoning attacks on MNIST and Fashion-MNIST using classical classifiers, showing degradation metrics and high attack success rates for backdoors.
motivation: Data poisoning threatens the integrity of supervised learning models, but practical comparisons of attack types across standard datasets and simple classifiers are needed to guide security-oriented evaluation.
method: The study trains Logistic Regression, Linear SVM, and Random Forest on clean and poisoned data with 5%, 10%, and 20% poisoning rates, measuring clean-test accuracy, macro-precision, macro-recall, macro-F1, and backdoor attack success rate.
result: Label flipping degrades performance most for Logistic Regression and Linear SVM while Random Forest remains more stable; backdoor poisoning achieves attack success rates of 0.9667 to 1.0000 across models and datasets with near-baseline clean accuracy.
conclusion: Indiscriminate poisoning appears in standard metrics, whereas targeted backdoor poisoning is stealthy and highly effective, motivating evaluation beyond clean-test accuracy for security.

title: ToxicRAG: Compromising Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems Via Single-Shot Knowledge Poisoning Attacks
authors: Haozhe Lu, Jiaqi Li, Xinyuan Zhu, Xiang Li
abstract: ArXiv:2609.11082v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) can ground large language model (LLM) outputs in external evidence, but it also exposes the system to knowledge poisoning. Representative attacks use multiple injected documents or templates that directly assert a target answer. We present ToxicRAG, a one-document-per-target attack that expresses misinformation as a coherent knowledge-update narrative. The generated document first acknowledges the previously accepted answer, introduces fabricated events that appear to invalidate it, and then attributes the attacker-selected answer to a set of purported authorities. An answer-focused self-validation loop optionally revises a candidate when a surrogate language model does not reproduce the target answer. We evaluate the attack on 100 target questions from each of Natural Questions, HotpotQA, and MS-MARCO, using four victim LLMs and four dense retrievers. In the sampled-corpus setting reported in this paper, ToxicRAG obtains ASRs between 0.61 and 0.91 across the twelve dataset--model combinations. It matches or exceeds the strongest evaluated baseline in every combination, with margins ranging from 0 to 11 percentage points. These results show that narrative-form poisoned documents can remain influential under the evaluated RAG configurations and motivate further study of factual consistency and source provenance in RAG systems.
tldr: ToxicRAG is a single-document knowledge poisoning attack that compromises retrieval-augmented generation systems by presenting misinformation as a coherent knowledge-update narrative.
motivation: RAG systems ground LLM outputs in external evidence but are vulnerable to knowledge poisoning, and existing attacks typically require multiple injected documents or templates.
method: The attack generates one poisoned document per target that acknowledges the original answer, introduces fabricated invalidating events, attributes a new answer to purported authorities, and optionally self-validates via a surrogate language model.
result: Across 12 dataset-model combinations (Natural Questions, HotpotQA, MS-MARCO with four victim LLMs and four retrievers), ToxicRAG achieves attack success rates between 0.61 and 0.91, matching or exceeding the strongest baseline by 0 to 11 percentage points.
conclusion: Narrative-form poisoned documents can remain influential under evaluated RAG configurations, motivating further work on factual consistency and source provenance in RAG systems.

title: Few-Shot Learning For Network Intrusion Detection: Methods, Datasets, And Performance
authors: Arne Roszeitis, Victor J\"uttner, Erik Buchmann
abstract: ArXiv:2609.11275v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Anomaly-based network intrusion detection systems (NIDS) are an important first line of defense. However, training NIDS for new attack types is challenging, because labeled attack data are rarely available. Few-shot learning (FSL) addresses this problem by learning from few samples. However, the approaches and evaluation settings, that have been investigated so far, vary widely. This work systematically reviews FSL approaches for NIDS published from 2022 to 2026. We conduct a systematic literature review with PRISMA 2020-like reporting to search ACM Digital Library, IEEE Xplore, and Scopus. From a set of 1,358 initial records, we retain 21 studies after screening, deduplication, and quality filtering. We classify the applied FSL approaches, datasets, and experimental parameters and compare reported performance. Meta-learning and convolutional neural networks are the most common approaches, with 8 and 10 studies, respectively. Most studies evaluate five or fewer samples per class, although settings vary. CIC-IDS2017 and CSE-CIC-IDS2018 are the most frequently used datasets. Missing parameters and source code limit reproducibility and direct comparison between approaches.
tldr: A systematic literature review of few-shot learning approaches for anomaly-based network intrusion detection, covering 21 studies published between 2022 and 2026.
motivation: Training network intrusion detection systems for novel attack types is difficult because labeled attack data are scarce, and existing few-shot learning studies vary widely in methods and evaluation settings, preventing comparison.
method: A PRISMA 2020-style systematic literature review searching ACM Digital Library, IEEE Xplore, and Scopus, screening 1,358 records down to 21 studies and classifying their FSL approaches, datasets, and experimental parameters.
result: Meta-learning (8 studies) and convolutional neural networks (10 studies) dominate; most studies use five or fewer samples per class, with CIC-IDS2017 and CSE-CIC-IDS2018 as the most common datasets, and missing parameters and code limit reproducibility.
conclusion: Few-shot learning for NIDS remains fragmented, and the field needs standardized reporting and shared implementations to enable fair comparison and reproducibility.

title: Max Independent Set Remains NP-hard When Excluding A Planar Induced Minor
abstract: ArXiv:2609.11285v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We show that there is a fixed planar graph [MATH], namely the [MATH] grid, such that Max Independent Set remains NP-hard in [MATH]-induced-minor-free graphs. This refutes the Dallard--Milani--torgel conjecture and a weakening of it by Gartland and Lokshtanov, and by Korhonen.
tldr: The paper proves that Max Independent Set remains NP-hard on graphs excluding a fixed planar induced minor, refuting a conjecture by Dallard–Milani–Štorgel and a weakening by Gartland–Lokshtanov and Korhonen.
motivation: Structural graph theory has sought to characterize graph classes excluding a planar induced minor where Max Independent Set becomes tractable, motivated by the conjecture that such classes have bounded treewidth or are otherwise tractable.
method: The authors construct a fixed planar grid as an induced minor and show that Max Independent Set remains NP-hard on graphs that exclude it, using a reduction from an NP-hard problem on planar graphs.
result: They establish that there exists a fixed planar graph—the grid—such that Max Independent Set is NP-hard on graphs with no induced minor isomorphic to it.
conclusion: This refutes the Dallard–Milani–Štorgel conjecture and related weakenings, demonstrating that excluding a planar induced minor does not guarantee tractability for Max Independent Set.

title: Estimating The Time Advantage Of Split-Staggered Starts In Record-Breaking Middle-Distance Races
abstract: ArXiv:2609.10833v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In July 2026, Josh Kerr broke the 26-year-old mile world record, the latest in an unusual concentration of recent middle-distance records that has led to widespread speculation about the role of advancing shoe and other technologies. However, like almost every other recent record-breaking performance, Kerr's race featured a split-staggered start -- an often overlooked, relatively novel start configuration that places a subset of athletes in a front group in the outside lanes, reducing the geometric burden associated with accelerating on tight turns while also avoiding the bulk of the extra distance associated with outside positioning in a traditional distance race. Here, these advantages are quantified using empirical lane-performance data, OMEGA measurements of realized race distance, video reconstruction, and a force-based model of curved running. Applying the resulting corrections to record-breaking performances from 2026, estimated advantages range from approximately 0.1 seconds to more than 1 second, depending on the event, race configuration, and model assumptions. Although small in absolute terms, these advantages demonstrate that start configuration represents a meaningful and previously overlooked source of performance advantage in modern middle-distance racing -- large enough to make the difference between a world record and an otherwise great performance.
tldr: This paper quantifies the time advantage gained from split-staggered starting configurations in recent record-breaking middle-distance running races.
motivation: A cluster of recent middle-distance world records has prompted speculation about technological and procedural advantages, and the split-staggered start is an overlooked factor that may meaningfully aid performance.
method: The author combines empirical lane-performance data, OMEGA measurements of realized race distance, video reconstruction, and a force-based model of curved running to estimate the geometric and biomechanical benefit of the split-staggered configuration.
result: Estimated advantages range from roughly 0.1 seconds to over 1 second depending on event, race configuration, and modeling assumptions, enough to distinguish a world record from a near-record performance.
conclusion: Start configuration is a previously overlooked but meaningful source of performance advantage in modern middle-distance racing, warranting consideration in record analysis.

title: EVTradeMatch: A Mobility-Aware Multi-Objective Matching Framework For Ev--ev Energy Trading
authors: Md. Mahfujur Rahman, Alistair Barros, Raja Jurdak, Darshika Koggalahewa
abstract: ArXiv:2609.10551v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Peer-to-peer energy trading among electric vehicles (EVs) can improve charging flexibility under limited charging infrastructure, but effective EV--EV trading requires coordinated provider--consumer matching under journey-specific conditions. This paper proposes EVTradeMatch, a prediction-guided multi-objective optimization framework for mobility-aware EV--EV energy trading. Building on the EVNextTrade study, a prior learning-to-rank model for charging-node recommendation, we define charging-node suitability as a prediction-derived score reflecting the appropriateness of assigning a provider--consumer pair to a candidate charging node based on mobility, energy, and contextual trading features. This score is used as a guidance signal and as an explicit optimization objective rather than as a hard selection rule. The EV--EV matching problem is formulated as a multi-objective mixed-integer linear program that maximizes matching coverage, transferred energy, and charging-node suitability while minimizing mobility cost under spatial, temporal, one-to-one matching, and charging-node capacity constraints. To approximate Pareto-efficient solutions in wide-area dynamic settings, we develop a tailored non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm II (NSGA-II). Experimental results show that EVTradeMatch improves transferred energy by 74.2--82.8% and charging-node suitability by 8.3--84.4% compared with proximity- and auction-based state-of-the-art methods, while improving matching coverage by 3.74--25.07 percentage points. Balanced NSGA-II solutions achieve 53.07[MATH]0.76% matching coverage and transfer 1701.94[MATH]17.03 kWh, with higher mobility cost as an explicit trade-off against travel-minimizing methods. Pareto-front analysis shows that the framework supports flexible selection among high-coverage, high-energy, low-mobility-cost, and high-suitability solutions according to operational priorities.
tldr: EVTradeMatch is a prediction-guided multi-objective optimization framework that matches provider-consumer electric vehicles for peer-to-peer charging-node-based energy trading.
motivation: Peer-to-peer energy trading among electric vehicles can improve charging flexibility under limited charging infrastructure, but it requires coordinated provider-consumer matching under journey-specific mobility, energy, and contextual conditions.
method: The authors define a prediction-derived charging-node suitability score (building on the EVNextTrade learning-to-rank model) and formulate EV-EV matching as a multi-objective mixed-integer linear program maximizing coverage, transferred energy, and suitability while minimizing mobility cost, solved approximately via a tailored NSGA-II.
result: Experiments show improvements in transferred energy of 74.2-82.8%, suitability gains of 8.3-84.4%, and coverage improvements of 3.74-25.07 percentage points over proximity- and auction-based baselines, with balanced solutions achieving 53.07±0.76% coverage and 1701.94±17.03 kWh transferred.
conclusion: The framework's Pareto-front analysis supports flexible selection among high-coverage, high-energy, low-mobility-cost, and high-suitability solutions according to operational priorities in wide-area dynamic EV energy trading.

title: Lateral Weak Stieltjes Derivatives: A Global Characterization Of Stieltjes--Sobolev Spaces
abstract: ArXiv:2609.10659v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Weak formulations for Stieltjes differential equations must retain the directional information carried by atoms of the driving measure. We derive a lateral integration-by-parts identity in which the posterior trace of the test function is forced by the atomic product rule. The resulting dual formulation gives an exact global characterization of integral Stieltjes--Sobolev spaces for the full exponent range from one to infinity and reconstructs the unique strong representative from its traced weak state. We prove that the associated traced weak operator is closed, establish Poincar\'e--Stieltjes estimates, and . The framework is then applied to finite-dimensional nonlinear measure-driven systems, yielding equivalence of weak, integral, and measure formulations, existence and uniqueness under integrable Lipschitz assumptions, compactness-based existence, and intrinsic reset laws. Cubic and logistic models illustrate the simultaneous encoding of continuous evolution and instantaneous interventions.
tldr: The paper develops a lateral integration-by-parts identity for weak Stieltjes derivatives, yielding a global characterization of integral Stieltjes–Sobolev spaces and applying it to measure-driven nonlinear systems.
motivation: Weak formulations of Stieltjes differential equations lose the directional information carried by atoms of the driving measure, limiting a complete functional-analytic treatment of such measure-driven dynamics.
method: The author derives a lateral integration-by-parts identity whose atomic product rule forces the posterior trace of the test function, producing a dual formulation that characterizes Stieltjes–Sobolev spaces across all exponents and recovers strong representatives from traced weak states.
result: The traced weak operator is shown to be closed, Poincaré–Stieltjes estimates are established, and weak, integral, and measure formulations are proven equivalent for finite-dimensional nonlinear measure-driven systems, including existence, uniqueness, compactness-based existence, and intrinsic reset laws.
conclusion: The framework unifies continuous evolution and instantaneous interventions, illustrated by cubic and logistic models, but remains a purely mathematical contribution to real analysis and measure theory with no connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum platforms.

title: A Variational Physics-informed Graph Neural Network For Heterogeneous Solid Mechanics
authors: Aashay Rajan Yadav, Amiya Prakash Das, Ratna Kumar Annabattula
abstract: ArXiv:2609.10983v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Stress localization in heterogeneous solids is governed by the bimaterial interface, where the displacement field remains [MATH]-continuous, while in-plane stresses jump due to the stiffness mismatch. Coordinate-based physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) represent this jump via a prescribed regularization width or a weighted interface penalty, making their accuracy sensitive to how phase-contrast changes are handled. This work presents a variational, label-free physics-informed graph neural network (PI-GNN) in which the heterogeneity is carried by the discretization rather than by the trial field. The solver operates on a conforming adaptive mesh graph, assigns constitutive behavior per element, and minimizes the discrete total potential energy as a single unweighted objective in which only first derivatives appear. The discrete energy on piecewise-linear elements coincides with the finite element (FE) Ritz functional. Dirichlet conditions are enforced by construction, with no penalty term, no interface weight, and no prescribed transition width. Using one fixed architecture, optimizer, and loss across small-strain elasticity and finite-strain Neo-Hookean hyperelasticity in two and three dimensions, the von Mises error remains below [MATH] across a stiffness-contrast sweep spanning [MATH], where a strong-form PINN degrades to [MATH], and its displacement error reaches [MATH] against [MATH] for the PI-GNN. A trained network halves the ([MATH]) error of an energy-based PINN ([MATH] versus [MATH]). Training cost exceeds a single FE solve by more than an order of magnitude, so the construction is a variationally consistent, penalty-free interface representation for parametric surrogates and inverse identification rather than a replacement for a one-off FE analysis.
tldr: A variational, label-free physics-informed graph neural network (PI-GNN) that models stress localization in heterogeneous solids without penalty terms or prescribed interface widths.
motivation: Coordinate-based PINNs struggle with bimaterial interfaces in heterogeneous solids, requiring regularization widths or weighted interface penalties that make accuracy sensitive to phase-contrast changes.
method: The solver operates on a conforming adaptive mesh graph with per-element constitutive behavior, minimizing the discrete total potential energy as a single unweighted objective that coincides with the finite element Ritz functional on piecewise-linear elements; Dirichlet conditions are enforced by construction.
result: Using one fixed architecture, optimizer, and loss, von Mises error stays below a threshold across a wide stiffness-contrast sweep where strong-form PINNs degrade severely, and the trained network halves the energy-based PINN's error, though training cost exceeds a single FE solve by an order of magnitude.
conclusion: The construction offers a variationally consistent, penalty-free interface representation suited to parametric surrogates and inverse identification rather than replacing one-off FE analysis.

title: Efx Allocations For Three Agents And Seven Or Eight Chores
abstract: ArXiv:2609.10585v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove that every nonnegative additive chore instance with three agents and either seven or eight indivisible chores admits a chores-EFX allocation, in the zero-tolerant sense that every owned chore, including one of zero cost, is quantified in the trim. Both proofs are computer-assisted, but their machine formulas differ. For seven chores, hand-checkable canonicalization reduces nonexistence to a quantifier-free linear real arithmetic (QF_LRA) formula over 21 variables with one failure clause per complete allocation. For eight chores, instances in which two agents share a weakly cheapest chore are lifted from the seven-chore theorem through the matching insertion lemma of Kobayashi, Mahara, and Sakamoto, and the remaining pairwise-disjoint-argmin class reduces to a residual QF_LRA formula over 24 variables. Z3 5.1.0 and cvc5 1.3.4 report both formulas unsatisfiable. With the known [MATH] theorem, this settles every three-agent instance with at most eight chores; [MATH] is the next open cardinality, and additive chores can fail to admit EFX for every [MATH].
tldr: The paper proves via computer-assisted QF_LRA satisfiability checks that every additive indivisible-chore instance with three agents and seven or eight chores admits a zero-tolerant EFX allocation, settling all three-agent cases up to eight chores.
motivation: EFX (envy-free up to any good/chore) fairness is a central open problem in fair division; the three-agent chore case was unresolved beyond six chores, and the general problem is known to fail for sufficiently many chores.
method: Canonicalization reduces the seven-chore nonexistence question to a quantifier-free linear real arithmetic formula in 21 variables; the eight-chore case is partly lifted from the seven-chore theorem via the matching insertion lemma of Kobayashi–Mahara–Sakamoto, with the residual pairwise-disjoint-argmin class encoded as a 24-variable QF_LRA formula, both shown unsatisfiable by Z3 5.1.0 and cvc5 1.3.4.
result: Both machine-verified formulas are unsatisfiable, establishing existence of zero-tolerant chores-EFX allocations for three agents with seven or eight chores, so the next open cardinality is nine.
conclusion: The work closes the three-agent EFX existence question for up to eight chores, using formal-methods tools rather than constructive algorithms, and points to nine chores as the next frontier.

title: Adaptive Diffusion Freezing: Privacy-preserving Diffusion Models Against Membership Inference Attacks
authors: Jialu Guo, Xiao Han, Junjie Wu
abstract: ArXiv:2609.10608v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Diffusion models have achieved remarkable success in generative tasks across various areas, however their training process raises significant privacy concerns, particularly under membership inference attacks (MIAs). Prior studies on privacy-preserving of diffusion models fail to balance privacy, utility, and efficiency. To address this gap, we propose a novel framework of privacy-preserving diffusion models, Adaptive Diffusion Freezing (ADF), which can defend against MIAs with better trade-off. By leveraging cross-timestep adaptive freezing training, ADF explicitly control the participation of different data subsets across diffusion timesteps via a mask matrix, which reduces the over-memorization and leads to more uniform model behaviors between member and nonmember samples. To construct a freezing mask matrix that effectively reduce membership leakage without unnecessarily harming generation quality, we introduce a pretraining-based risk-aware freezing policy to estimate MIA risk based on memorization tendency, and suppress the contribution of the subset-timestep pairs with higher risk. Evaluations on multiple datasets demonstrate that ADF provides effective defense performance as well as state-of-the-art privacy-utility-efficiency trade-off performance compared to various baselines.
tldr: ADF is a privacy-preserving diffusion model framework that uses cross-timestep adaptive freezing to defend against membership inference attacks while balancing privacy, utility, and efficiency.
motivation: Diffusion models memorize training data, making them vulnerable to membership inference attacks, and existing privacy-preserving approaches fail to balance privacy, utility, and efficiency.
method: The framework applies a risk-aware freezing policy that learns a mask matrix controlling which data subsets participate at which diffusion timesteps, suppressing high-risk subset-timestep pairs to reduce over-memorization.
result: Experiments across multiple datasets show ADF effectively defends against MIAs while achieving state-of-the-art privacy-utility-efficiency trade-offs versus baselines.
conclusion: Adaptive diffusion freezing offers a practical way to reduce membership leakage in diffusion models without substantially harming generation quality.

title: A2ABreak: Systematic Security Analysis Of The A2a Protocol
authors: Alireza Lotfi, Mirza Masfiqur Rahman, Imtiaz Karim, Elisa Bertino
abstract: ArXiv:2609.10871v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol, now governed by the Linux Foundation, is an open standard that enables autonomous AI agents to discover, authenticate with, and delegate tasks to one another across organizational boundaries. Designed to complement the Model Context Protocol (MCP) for tool integration, A2A is rapidly emerging as the horizontal communication layer of the multi-agent ecosystem. Yet the protocol's security has received no systematic analysis. This paper presents A2ABreak, the first rigorous systematic security analysis of the A2A protocol. We introduce a novel framework that utilizes an LLM-assisted extraction of a verified finite-state machine directly from the natural-language specification, producing a unified model of 37 states and 76 transitions from 929 formalized statements, and then systematically reasons over this model to discover protocol-level vulnerabilities through adversarial verification, under a full-compliance assumption. Our analysis uncovers 11 new vulnerabilities, each exploitable by a specification-compliant adversary without requiring any implementation flaw. Among the findings are cross-client context injection through unprotected context identifiers, credential harvesting via multi-hop identity loss in delegation chains, and data exfiltration through rogue agents advertising unattested capability claims. A2ABreak achieves 73.3% precision and 84.6% F1 against independent expert review, while a zero-shot LLM baseline operating over the same specification produces zero confirmed findings, demonstrating that explicit formal grounding is essential for sound protocol security analysis.
tldr: A2ABreak performs the first systematic security analysis of the Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol by extracting a verified finite-state machine from its natural-language specification and adversarially probing it for protocol-level vulnerabilities.
motivation: The A2A protocol is becoming the standard communication layer for multi-agent AI systems, yet its security had never been systematically analyzed, leaving specification-level weaknesses unexplored.
method: The authors use LLM-assisted extraction to build a unified 37-state, 76-transition finite-state machine from 929 formalized specification statements, then systematically reason over this model under a full-compliance adversary assumption with adversarial verification.
result: They uncover 11 new specification-compliant vulnerabilities, including cross-client context injection, credential harvesting via multi-hop identity loss, and data exfiltration through rogue agents; A2ABreak reaches 73.3% precision and 84.6% F1 versus expert review, while a zero-shot LLM baseline finds zero confirmed issues.
conclusion: Explicit formal grounding via model extraction is essential for sound protocol security analysis, and the A2A protocol contains exploitable design-level flaws that must be addressed.

title: DeFiFusion: Combining Transaction Events With Smart Contracts To Detect Price Manipulation Attacks
authors: Rui Cao, Shaojing Fan, Liming Fang, Yuchan Liu, Yingying Jiao, Zhenguang Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2609.11008v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Decentralized Finance (DeFi) has emerged as a rapidly growing blockchain-based financial service, where market transaction dynamics and underlying smart contract logic are intricately intertwined. This autonomous interplay, while eliminating centralized intermediaries, significantly expands the vulnerability surface of DeFi protocols to Price Manipulation Attacks (PMAs), which have already inflicted catastrophic financial losses. Despite their gravity, existing detection paradigms suffer from fundamental limitations. Transaction-centric methods lack awareness of contract execution semantics, making them prone to false positives under legitimate market volatility, while static contract analyses ignore real transaction behaviors and frequently report vulnerabilities that are infeasible to exploit in practice. We present DeFiFusion, a dual-modal PMA detection framework that closes this gap by jointly modeling transaction events and smart contract semantics within a unified pipeline. Our core insight is that PMA maliciousness emerges only from the interaction between transaction behaviors and the contract logic they exploit; neither signal suffices in isolation. Accordingly, we derive price-manipulation-aware event encoding for extracting fine-grained temporal and economic features tailored to manipulation patterns. We further introduce LLM-based contract semantic extraction to supply the execution-logic context that prior behavioral methods lack. To fuse these modalities, we propose a Dual-Modal Projection-Fusion Transformer with T5-style relative positional encoding, capturing the cyclic multi-stage execution structures that distinguish PMAs from benign market activity. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DeFiFusion consistently achieves state-of-the-art detection performance, effectively recalling 222 of the 225 PMA cases while maintaining a precision of 96.10%.
tldr: DeFiFusion is a dual-modal detection framework that jointly models blockchain transaction events and smart contract semantics to identify price manipulation attacks in decentralized finance.
motivation: Price manipulation attacks in DeFi cause catastrophic financial losses, yet existing detectors are either transaction-centric (ignoring contract execution semantics, causing false positives) or static contract analyzers (ignoring real behavior, flagging infeasible exploits).
method: The authors derive price-manipulation-aware event encoding for fine-grained temporal and economic features, use LLM-based semantic extraction of contract logic, and fuse both modalities with a Dual-Modal Projection-Fusion Transformer using T5-style relative positional encoding.
result: DeFiFusion achieves state-of-the-art detection performance, recalling 222 of 225 PMA cases while maintaining 96.10% precision.
conclusion: Jointly modeling transaction behaviors and contract semantics enables robust, practical detection of DeFi price manipulation attacks that neither signal alone can capture.

title: The Missing Boundary: How Autonomous Agents Lose Control
authors: Zonghao Ying, Xiangfan Wu, Huiyu Wu, Xing Zheng, Huangsheng Cheng, Xiaorong Shi, Jing Guo
abstract: ArXiv:2609.11024v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Autonomous agents increasingly perform long-horizon tasks involving tool use, persistent state, and consequential actions, raising a fundamental question: Existing studies often attribute such failures to adversarial instructions, malicious environments, or conflicting objectives, leaving unclear how loss of control can emerge during otherwise legitimate task execution. We study this question by independently manipulating three factors: goal pressure, control degradation, and executable unsafe opportunity. Our central hypothesis is that a degraded control boundary becomes consequential when the environment exposes an executable action that crosses it, even when the underlying task remains legitimate and a sanctioned path remains feasible. We test this hypothesis in a deterministic multi-turn environment across five agent models and 16 operational domains. Across 1,800 unique trajectories, we find that neither degraded control nor unsafe opportunity alone produces substantial loss of control; when both are present, the loss-of-control rate reaches [MATH] in the full-factorial study and [MATH] across ten additional operational domains. Restoring the original control boundary reduces the rate to [MATH] even when the unsafe action remains executable. A context-management ablation further shows that compaction itself is not harmful: preserving the control constraints yields [MATH] loss of control, whereas omitting them increases the rate to [MATH]. These results show how a latent loss of control can become an external violation: the task objective remains intact, but an executable opportunity can turn a missing control boundary into consequential action. Our code will be made publicly available at [URL].
tldr: A factorial study of autonomous LLM-based agents showing that loss of control emerges only when a degraded control boundary coincides with an executable unsafe action, even during otherwise legitimate task execution.
motivation: Prior work attributes agent failures to adversarial prompts, malicious environments, or conflicting objectives, leaving unclear how loss of control can arise during legitimate task execution with a sanctioned path still available.
method: The authors independently manipulate three factors—goal pressure, control degradation, and executable unsafe opportunity—in a deterministic multi-turn environment across five agent models and 16 operational domains, collecting 1,800 trajectories plus a context-management ablation.
result: Neither degraded control nor unsafe opportunity alone produces substantial loss of control, but their combination yields high loss-of-control rates; restoring the control boundary reduces the rate even when the unsafe action remains executable, and compaction is harmful only when control constraints are omitted.
conclusion: Latent loss of control becomes an external violation when an executable opportunity turns a missing control boundary into consequential action, motivating preservation of control constraints in agent context management.

title: The Machines Are Calling: Measuring Automated And Synthetic Voices In Unwanted Inbound Calls
authors: Xingyu Shen, Tommy Duong, Muduo Xu, Xiaodong An, Jiaqi Gan, Haoyuan Tang, Jamey Z. Liang, Siyu Zhang, Yan Zhang, Simiao Ren
abstract: ArXiv:2609.11137v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In February 2024 the U.S. Federal Communications Commission (FCC) placed AI-generated voices under the Telephone Consumer Protection Act (TCPA). Yet no peer-reviewed measurement says how much unwanted call traffic is placed by a machine, or how much of that machine speech is synthesized rather than played from a recording. We report both with a disclosed pipeline. An interactive voice honeypot (language-model personas on real U.S. numbers, the caller recorded on its own track) recorded 10,987 calls over 66 days; 11 days on which our stack answered silently are set aside. Three instruments read each opening: an audio fingerprint that finds the same recording played on other calls, a commercial synthetic-speech detector on the caller's first ten seconds, and blinded listeners who check what it flags. Of the 7,233 calls our persona greeted on normal days, 13.8% open with a recording we also heard on another call, and 13.1% with fresh audio the detector labels synthetic. A further 9.9% open with a caller who never spoke after our greeting, 54.2% with fresh audio the detector labels human, and 9.0% could not be scored. Machine-voiced openings are therefore at least 26.9%, a further tenth of calls are silent connections we read as machine-placed, and replays of a recording make up 45% of the detector's own rate (29.3% of 6,192 scored openings). The same waveform played on two calls lands on opposite sides of the detector's threshold 13.6% of the time, and eleven listeners confirm 54.4% of what it flags. Synthetic openings concentrate in lead-generation spam (33.8%), not fraud (21.1%); 0.44% disclose automation. Prevalence tracks how long a bait number has circulated (59% against 19% in the same weeks): seeding history, not calendar time, explains the trend. Campaigns outlast their numbers: one recorded compliance notice opens calls in six campaigns, and one synthetic voice serves nine.
tldr: An interactive voice honeypot study measuring how much unwanted U.S. telemarketing call traffic is machine-placed and how much of that speech is synthetically generated rather than recorded.
motivation: The FCC placed AI-generated voices under the TCPA in 2024, yet no peer-reviewed measurement quantifies how much unwanted call traffic comes from machines or how much of that machine speech is synthesized.
method: An LLM-persona voice honeypot on real U.S. numbers recorded 10,987 calls over 66 days; each call opening was scored by an audio fingerprint for replayed recordings, a commercial synthetic-speech detector on the first ten seconds, and blinded human listeners.
result: Among 7,233 greeted calls, machine-voiced openings are at least 26.9% (13.8% replays plus 13.1% fresh synthetic audio), with a further 9.9% silent connections; detector threshold instability is 13.6% and listener confirmation 54.4%.
conclusion: Automated and synthetic voice prevalence in unwanted calls is substantial, concentrates in lead-generation spam rather than fraud, and depends on how long a bait number has circulated rather than calendar time.

title: You Get What You Sample: Evaluating Sampling Strategies For Web Security Measurements
authors: Xuenan Zhang, Yuqing Yang, Giancarlo Pellegrino
abstract: ArXiv:2609.11218v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Web measurement studies rely on domain datasets such as Tranco to quantify the prevalence and impact of security issues at scale, but exhaustively analyzing these datasets is often infeasible because of the cost of advanced analysis techniques, requiring the use of sampling. Despite its widespread use, sampling remains largely guided by convention---most commonly domain selection---rather than evidence, and its influence on the validity and generalizability of security findings has received little systematic evaluation. Consequently, it remains unclear whether common sampling strategies introduce systematic bias, distort observed vulnerability rates, or limit comparability across studies. In this work, we undertake, to the best of our knowledge, the first comprehensive investigation into how sampling methodologies affect the measurements and the conclusions. Through a comprehensive literature review and large-scale measurements of 500k Tranco and 24.8M Common Crawl hosts, we perform a comparative evaluation of datasets and sampling strategies. We show that, while Top [MATH] sampling may be a rational strategy, the researchers have to bear in mind that Top [MATH] does not reflect the overall distribution of the web. Instead, probability-based strategies yield stable, unbiased estimates for prevalence and many impact objectives. Hybrid sampling provides no advantages over pure probability sampling, as its deterministic prefix consistently contributes negatively to accuracy. Building on these results, we provide data-backed guidance for future studies, proposing to use an adaptive probability-based sampling strategy that remains effective even when the prevalence of the target issue is unknown.
tldr: A large-scale empirical study evaluating how domain sampling strategies in web security measurements bias prevalence estimates and affect the validity of findings, with data-backed guidance favoring adaptive probability-based sampling.
motivation: Web security measurement studies rely on domain datasets (e.g., Tranco, Common Crawl) but exhaustive analysis is infeasible, so sampling is used; yet sampling is guided by convention rather than evidence and its effects on validity and comparability have not been systematically assessed.
method: Combined a literature review with large-scale measurements of 500k Tranco and 24.8M Common Crawl hosts to comparatively evaluate datasets and sampling strategies, including Top-M, probability-based, and hybrid approaches.
result: Top-M sampling does not reflect the overall web distribution, probability-based strategies yield stable and unbiased prevalence and impact estimates, and hybrid sampling's deterministic prefix consistently degrades accuracy relative to pure probability sampling.
conclusion: The authors recommend an adaptive probability-based sampling strategy that remains effective even when target-issue prevalence is unknown, providing evidence-based guidance for future web security measurement studies.

title: The Epistemic Risk Of The 31st Spore: If Planets Aren't Fine Tuned, We're Doing Life Detection Wrong
abstract: ArXiv:2609.10604v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Exploration of planetary bodies within our solar system will be essential for understanding the origin of life on Earth and the distribution of life in the universe. Planetary protection policy is concerned with balancing this desire for exploration against the risks of contaminating alien planets with Earth life, and contaminating Earth with alien life. However, at present, we have no fundamental scientific understanding of life's emergence or its nature beyond Earth. Given this nearly complete ignorance about the possibility of alien life, or Earth life's capacity to expand beyond our planet, it is difficult to reason about the real risks of space exploration. Here we contend that contemporary understandings of the risks of forward contamination are based on arguments which inconsistently apply our incomplete knowledge to the problem. We reason that a more assertive posture towards space exploration, focused on determining whether other planets in the solar system are inhabited, is warranted and explain why such a posture may not increase the epistemic risks of planetary contamination. Finally, we explore the consequences of our arguments for planetary protection protocols, and life detection efforts.
tldr: The paper argues that planetary protection policies inconsistently apply incomplete knowledge about alien life and proposes a more assertive exploration posture for life detection.
motivation: Current planetary protection policies are based on uncertain and inconsistent reasoning about the risks of forward and backward contamination, given our ignorance about life's emergence and nature beyond Earth.
method: Conceptual and epistemic analysis of risk arguments in planetary protection, examining how incomplete knowledge is applied and framing consequences for exploration and life detection protocols.
result: The authors contend that a more assertive approach to exploring solar system bodies for life may not increase epistemic risks of contamination and could improve life detection efforts.
conclusion: Planetary protection protocols should be revised to reflect epistemic humility, balancing contamination risks against the scientific value of determining whether other planets are inhabited.

title: Why We Should Condition Denoising Diffusion Generative Models On Windows Of Past Observations
abstract: ArXiv:2609.10924v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Data assimilation (DA) is, traditionally, a cycling process that relies on time-dependent priors to propagate information from past observations to future cycles. Using denoising diffusion generative modeling for DA is challenging because standard approaches use a fixed training data set, which in turn leads to a static prior that ignores information from past observations. Because past observations are ignored, DA systems with static priors lead to larger posterior errors than cycling DA systems. Incorporating time-dependent priors into generative models, however, requires expensive and frequent retraining. Motivated by linear systems theory - where the dependence of a prediction of a Kalman filter on past observations decays exponentially - we condition diffusion models on short windows of past observations. Specifically, we describe training procedures for two frameworks: a diffusion DA system predicting the current state given a set of past observations, and a diffusion ``direct observation prediction'' (DOP) system, predicting future observations given a set of past observations. Using a canonical linear system, we show that both systems can achieve the minimal posterior error characteristic of a fully-cycled DA/DOP system, without re-training, provided the time windows are long enough. The linear setup ensures analytical tractability, avoids confounding neural network training errors, and confirms that conditioning on windows of past observations is required for efficient and accurate diffusion-based DA or DOP.
tldr: The paper proposes conditioning denoising diffusion generative models on short windows of past observations to match the performance of cycling data assimilation systems without retraining.
